# Why 21? Minimum Drinking Age Saves Lives

Underage drinking facts prove the need for the  
minimum legal drinking age.

Why is 21 the Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA)?

More than 25,000 lives have been saved in the U.S. thanks to the MLDA. This law continues to curb teen drinking and prevent tragedies—decreasing crashes by an estimated 16 percent and keeping young people safe.

Why do we make young people wait until 21 to drink alcohol?

Many activities have ages of initiation. A person must wait until age 16 to start driving, age 18 to marry without parental consent, age 35 to become president and so on.

The age limit for alcohol is based on research which shows that young people react differently to alcohol. Teens get drunk twice as fast as adults, 9 but have more trouble knowing when to stop. Teens naturally overdo it and binge more often than adults.

 

Enforcing the legal drinking age of 21 reduces traffic crashes involving drunk teens, 4-6 protects young people’s maturing brains,12,14 and keeps young people safer overall.

###### References 4. Fell, J.; “Minimum Legal Drinking Age Policy Knowledge Asset,” website created by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation’s Substance Abuse Policy Research Program; March 2009. 6. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, National Center for Statistics and Analysis “Lives Saved in 2012 by Restraint Use and Minimum Drinking Age Laws” DOT HS 811 851 A Brief Statistical Summary 2013. [Read More](http://www-nrd.nhtsa.dot.gov/Pubs/811851.pdf) 12. Shults, Ruth A., Elder, Randy W., Sleet, David A., Nichols, James L., Alao, Mary O. Carande-Kulis, Vilma G., Zaza, Stephanie, Sosin, Daniel M., Thompson, Robert S., and the Task Force on Community Preventive Services. “Reviews of Evidence Regarding Interventions to Reduce Alcohol-Impaired Driving.” Am J Prev Med 2001;21(4S). [Read More](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/)  14. Zeigler DW, Wang CC, Yoast RA, Dickinson BD, Mccaffree MA, Robinowitz CB, et al. The Neurocognitive Effects of Alcohol on Adolescents and College Students. Prev Med 2005 Jan;40(1):23-32.  [Read More](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15530577)

How many children under the age of 12 try marijuana each day in the U.S.?

Children as young as nine years old already start viewing alcohol in a more positive way, and approximately 3,300 kids as young as 12 try marijuana each day. 

References  
Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. (2018). Key substance use and mental health indicators in the United States: Results from the 2017 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (HHS Publication No. SMA 18-5068, NSDUH Series H-53). Rockville, MD: Center for Behavioral Health Statistics and Quality, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

What percentage of teens have tried alcohol? +

About 30 percent of 8th graders have tried alcohol.   
 

###### References Johnston, L. D., Miech, R. A., O’Malley, P. M., Bachman, J. G., Schulenberg, J. E., & Patrick, M. E. (2020). Monitoring the Future national survey results on drug use 1975-2019: Overview, key findings on adolescent drug use. Ann Arbor: Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan.

How does underage drinking affect teens as they get older?

Youth who start drinking before age 15 years are six times more likely to develop alcohol dependence or abuse later in life than those who begin drinking at or after age 21 years.

References  
Center for Behavioral Health Statistics and Quality. 2015 National Survey on Drug Use and Health: Detailed Tables. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Rockville, MD; 2016.

How many people become addicted to cannabis?

About 1 in 10 cannabis users will become addicted. For people who begin using before the  

age of 18, that number rises to 1 in 6.

###### References Lopez-Quintero, C, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC). Drug Alcohol Depend. 115(1-2): p. 120-30

How common is it that kids drink and do drugs?

1 in 3 youth who drink alcohol have also combined alcohol with cannabis on the same evenings. On these occasions, they tend to experience 2-3 times more problems compared to those when they only consume alcohol. 

###### References Mallett, K.A., Turrisi, R., Hultgren, B.A., Sell, N., Reavy, R., & Cleveland, M. (2017). When alcohol is only part of the problem: An event-level analysis of negative consequences related to alcohol and other substance use. Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, 31(3), 307-314. PMCID: PMC5422123.

Would lowering the legal drinking age make alcohol less of a big deal, and less attractive to teens?

History says no. When states had lower legal drinking ages in the U.S., the underage drinking problem was worse.3 For example, before the 21 minimum legal drinking age was implemented by all states, teens drinking and driving were involved in over twice as many fatal traffic crashes as today.3

References  
3. Fell, James. From “Chapter 2: Federalism: Resolved, the Federal Government should restore each State’s freedom to set its drinking age.” in Ellis, Richard and Nelson, Michael (eds.) Debating Reform. CQPress Publishers, Fall 2009.

Can’t parents teach their teens how to drink alcohol responsibly by giving them small amounts-under supervision-before they reach 21?

Some states permit parents to do this with their own child (rarely, if ever, with someone else’s child), but there’s no evidence that this approach actually works.3 As matter of fact, there is evidence to contrary. When teens feel they have their parents’ approval to drink, they do it more and more often when they are not with their parents. When parents have concrete, enforced rules about alcohol, according to binge drinking statistics, young people binge drink less. However, kids who are simply more connected with their parents, for example, who attend family dinners more frequently, are less likely to drink alcohol or use other drugs among other risk factors.7

References  
3. Fell, James. From “Chapter 2: Federalism: Resolved, the Federal Government should restore each State’s freedom to set its drinking age.” in Ellis, Richard and Nelson, Michael (eds.) Debating Reform. CQPress Publishers, Fall 2009.  
7. Fulkerson, J.A., Story, M., Mellin, A., Leffert, N., Neumark-Sztainer, D., & French, S.A. (2006). Family Dinner Meal Frequency and Adolescent Development: Relationships with Developmental Assets and High-Risk Behaviors. Journal of Adolescent Health, 39(3), 337-345.; Eisenberg, M.E., Neumark-Sztainer, D., Fulkerson, J.A., & Story, M. (2008). Family meals and substance use: is there a long-term protective association? Journal of Adolescent Health, 43(2), 151-156.; Fulkerson, J.A., Kubik, M.Y., Story, M., Lytle, L., & Arcan, C. (2009). Are there nutritional and other benefits associated with family meals among at-risk youth? Journal of Adolescent Health, 45(4), 389-395.; Skeer, M.R., & Ballard, E.L. (2013). Are family meals as good for youth as we think they are? A review of the literature on family meals as they pertain to adolescents’ risk prevention. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 42(7), 943-963; Perasso, G., Carone, N., Health Behavior in School Aged Children Lombardy Group 2014, & Barone, L. (2019). Alcohol consumption in adolescence: the role of adolecents’ gender, parental control, and family dinners attendance in an Italian HBSC sample. Journal of Family Studies, 1-13.

History of the Minimum Legal Drinking Age Act

On July 17, 1984, President Ronald Reagan signed the Minimum Legal Drinking Age-21 Law, alongside drunk driving victims and survivors from MADD, then-U.S. Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole, and Congressional sponsors. Over the last four decades, this landmark federal law has served as a blueprint for MADD’s efforts to end impaired driving.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates approximately 800 to 900 lives are saved every year as a result of setting the minimum legal drinking age in the U.S. at 21.

![President Ronald Reagan signs the Minimum Legal Drinking Age-21 Law, alongside drunk driving victims and survivors from MADD, then-U.S. Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole, and Congressional sponsors](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

Myth & Facts

There are many unfortunate and dangerous myths when it comes to underage use of alcohol and other drugs. Click on each myth below to learn the truth and the facts that support it.

MYTH: MADD is working to eliminate teen drunk driving rather than focusing on underage drinking prevention efforts.

False. One of MADD’s pillars is promoting zero tolerance for underage drinking.

Kids who start drinking young are seven times more likely to be in an alcohol-related crash according to underage drinking statistics. MADD knows that by preventing underage drinking today, we can end drunk driving tomorrow. 

###### 

##### References  Hingson, Ralph, et al. “Age of Drinking Onset, Driving After Drinking, and Involvement in Alcohol-Related Motor Vehicle Crashes.” DOT HS 809 188. Washington, DC: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, January 2001. [Read More](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11789578/)

MYTH: Europeans let their kids drink at an early age, yet they do not have the alcohol-related problems we do.

Actually, in Europe, young people have higher intoxication rates than in the United States, and less than a quarter had lower or equivalent rates to the United States. Also, a greater percentage of young people in the majority of Europe report binge drinking at higher rates than compared to their US counterparts.1-2Most European youth have higher rates of alcohol-related problems because of their heavy drinking. 

 

Perhaps the best example of fact versus myth is what happened in New Zealand. In 1999, New Zealand lowered its purchase age from 20 to 18. Not only did drunk driving crashes increase, but youth started to drink earlier, binge drinking escalated, and in the 12 months following the decrease in legal drinking age, there was a 50 percent increase in drunk teens, 18- and 19-year-old patients, at the Auckland Hospital emergency room.3

##### References 1. The ESPAD Report 2003.  Alcohol and Other Drug Use Among Students in 35 European Countries.  Published 2004. [Read excerpts here.](http://www.monitoringthefuture.org/pubs/espadusa2003.pdf) 2. Johnston, L. D., O’Malley, P. M., Bachman, J. G., & Schulenberg, J. E. (2004). Monitoring the Future national results on adolescent drug use: Overview of key findings, 2003 (NIH Publication No. 04-5506). Bethesda, MD: National Institute on Drug Abuse. [Read the overview here. 3. Kyrpi, Kypros, et al.  “Minimum Purchasing Age for Alcohol and Traffic Crash Injuries Among 15- to 19-Year-Olds in New Zealand.” American Journal of Public Health, January 2006, Voi 96, No. 1. Read the Study Here](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1470436/) .

MYTH: Alcohol is not that big of a deal anymore. Shouldn’t I be more worried about other more dangerous drugs?

Teen alcohol use kills 4,300 people each year—that’s more than all illegal drugs combined. 

 

##### References Sacks JJ, Gonzales KR, Bouchery EE, Tomedi LE, Brewer RD. 2010 National and State Costs of Excessive Alcohol Consumption. Am J Prev Med 2015; 49(5):e73–e79. [Read More](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26477807/)

MYTH: The law only makes youth want to drink because it’s a “forbidden fruit.”

When the “forbidden fruit” is no longer forbidden, youth simply drink more. In states where the drinking age was 18, teens statistically drank more than in states where the minimum drinking age was 21. They continued to drink more as adults in their early 20s.4 

 

##### References 4. Maisto, S.A., & Rachal, J.V. (1980). Indications of the relationship between adolescent drinking practices, related behaviors, and drinking age law: An examination of data from a national sample. In H. Wechsler (Ed.), Minimum drinking age laws: An evaluation (pp.155-176). Lexington, MA: D.C. Heath & Co.

MYTH: Lowering the drinking age will encourage young people to be responsible consumers rather than drink at uncontrolled, private parties.

Many youth drink with the goal to get drunk. They are not “wired” in the brain to assess risk and to be responsible when it comes to risky behavior. There is no class or situation that will prompt a teen to drink responsibly when alcohol flows freely.

MYTH: Drinking is just a phase all kids go through; they’ll grow out of it.

Actually, many don’t. In fact, the earlier someone begins drinking, the more likely they are to be alcohol dependent in later life. More than 40 percent of individuals who start drinking before the age of 13 will develop alcohol abuse or alcohol dependence at some point in their lives.5 Ninety-five percent of the 14 million people who are alcohol dependent began drinking before the legal age of 21.6 

 

##### References 5. Grant, Bridgett and Deborah Dawson. “Age at Onset of Alcohol Use and Its Association with DSM-IV Alcohol Abuse and Dependence.” Results from the National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey.  Journal of Substance Abuse 9 (1997): 103-110. 6. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. “Alcohol Dependence or Abuse and Age at First Use.” Washington, DC: Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Applied Studies, October 22, 2004.

MYTH: If I’m old enough to go to war, I should be old enough to drink.

21 is the minimum age because a person’s brain does not stop developing until his or her early to mid-20s. Drinking alcohol while the brain is still developing can lead to long-lasting deficits in cognitive abilities, including learning and memory. 

 

Alcohol use by those under 21 is also related to numerous health problems including injuries and death resulting from alcohol poisoning, car crashes, suicide, homicide, assaults, drowning, and recreational mishaps. Not to mention that the early onset of drinking by youth significantly increases the risk of future health problems such as addiction. 

 

Regardless of a person’s profession, underage drinking is still dangerous and unsafe. It is a fact based on biology not maturity or service to our country. 

 

##### References  How alcohol affects brain: <https://pubs.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/aa63/aa63.htm>   Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. “Alcohol Dependence or Abuse and Age at First Use.” Washington, DC: Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Applied Studies, October 22, 2004.

MYTH: MADD says kids shouldn’t have access to marijuana, but marijuana isn’t as bad as alcohol, I mean at least it is not addictive.

Marijuana is very addictive! In fact, in 2016 over 4 million people were diagnosed with substance use disorder due to marijuana use. Marijuana that is produced and sold now has a much higher content of THC than what was seen on the market in the 60’s and 70’s. Just like with alcohol, the young brain is not ready to protect teens against drugs like marijuana. 

 

##### References  Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. (2017). Key substance use and mental health indicators in the United States: Results from the 2016 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (HHS Publication No. SMA 17-5044, NSDUH Series H-52). Rockville, MD: Center for Behavioral Health Statistics and Quality, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. Retrieved from <https://www.samhsa.gov/data/>  Citation: NIDA. Marijuana. National Institute on Drug Abuse website.  <https://www.drugabuse.gov/publications/drugfacts/marijuana>. Updated August 1, 2017.

You Can Help Prevent Child and Teen Substance Abuse

People who start drinking or doing drugs at an early age can face severe, persistent problems throughout their lives. Whether you are a parent or a teen, you have the power to make a difference.

[Learn More](https://madd.org/underage-substance-use/)

## Our Mission

MADD’s mission is to end drunk and drugged driving, support the victims of these violent crimes, and prevent underage drinking and other drug use.

## About MADD

One woman’s courageous fight against drunk driving sparked a movement that transformed our nation for decades. We carry that mission forward, invigorated by the possibility that together, we can end impaired driving in our lifetime. This requires collective change; sharing the responsibility of protecting one another from harm.

MADD champions anti-drunk driving technology, leads prevention efforts across all communities in the U.S., supports victims and survivors, and advocates for stricter laws. To make impaired driving a thing of the past we must continue to change behaviors and fundamentally shift how future generations think about road safety.

To learn more about MADD’s impact, read our [**2025 Annual Impact Report**.](https://online.flippingbook.com/view/282756840/)

![45th Anniversary Group Photo](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

### The HALT Drunk Driving Law - Anti-Drunk Driving Technology for All

MADD’s bold and achievable goal is that every new car will be equipped with anti-drunk driving technology by 2030, setting us on a path to end drunk driving for good. Once in place, this technology is expected to save more than 10,000 lives per year and prevent hundreds of thousands of injuries. MADD victims and survivors worked with a bipartisan group of Members of Congress, representatives of the auto industry, and the U.S. Department of Transportation on this advanced impaired driving prevention technology for 16 years before it came to fruition.

[Learn More About the HALT Act](https://madd.org/haltact/)

## People Served

**51%**

Since our founding in 1980, MADD has helped to cut drunk driving deaths by approximately 51%.

**500,000**

MADD helped save nearly 500,000 lives in that time —  this is why we do what we do. [Read our Impact Report](https://online.flippingbook.com/view/282756840/).

**1M**

And as of December 2023, MADD has supported nearly one million (930,226) victims with our [services](https://madd.org/victim-assistance/?_ga=2.92655582.2146484293.1728336633-1771597186.1680720734).

## Victim Services

We provide vital services at no cost to impaired driving victims, survivors, and their loved ones through emotional support, guidance, and information about the criminal and civil justice process. These resources include:

* Court accompaniment and advocacy services
* Information about victims’ rights and education on topics related to victimization
* Assistance finding national and local financial resources
* Direct and indirect emotional support options, including one-on-one emotional support, peer support groups, and referrals for therapy

[Get Help](https://madd.org/victim-assistance/)

Mothers Against Drunk Driving has more than 65 offices across America, Puerto Rico, and Canada. We invite you to get connected in your area to help put an end to impaired driving for good.

### 21 + Prevention Programs

[MADD’s 21+ Prevention Program](https://madd.org/why-21/) aims to educate adults about [safe alternatives](https://madd.org/drunk-driving/safe-ride/) to drinking and driving including rideshare, designated drivers, and public transportation. We also work to ensure consistent sentencing in the criminal justice system through our court monitoring program to deter offenders from getting behind the wheel impaired.

args.summary:
Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD) is a nonprofit organization founded in 1980 with a mission to end drunk and drugged driving, support victims of these crimes, and prevent underage drinking and other drug use. Since its founding, MADD has helped cut drunk driving deaths by approximately 51% and saved nearly 500,000 lives. As of December 2023, MADD has supported nearly one million victims (930,226) with its services.

Key initiatives include the HALT Drunk Driving Law, which aims to equip every new car with anti-drunk driving technology by 2030, expected to save more than 10,000 lives per year. The organization notes that 33 people are killed and 943 people are injured daily in preventable drunk driving crashes in the U.S. Kids who start drinking young are 7 times more likely to be in an alcohol-related crash.

MADD provides victim services at no cost, including court accompaniment, advocacy, victims' rights education, assistance finding financial resources, and emotional support options. The organization has over 65 offices across America, Puerto Rico, and Canada. Prevention programs include the Power of Parents and Power of Youth programs for underage substance use prevention, and 21+ prevention programs promoting safe alternatives to drinking and driving such as rideshare and designated drivers. MADD also operates MADD Sports, leveraging athletes to raise awareness about impaired driving.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)Abstract

Using blood alcohol level data from fatal crashes involving youthful drivers in the United States from the years 1982 through 1997, we performed a pooled cross-sectional time-series analysis to evaluate the effects of laws establishing lower BAC limits and restricting alcohol usage for these youths. After accounting for differences among the 50 states in various background factors, changes in demographic factors within states over time, and the effects of other related laws, results indicate substantial reductions in alcohol-positive involvement in fatal crashes attributable to these youth-specific laws.

* * *

The United States, in contrast to most of the other industrialized nations of Europe and the Far East, makes a significant effort to prevent drinking by youths under age 21. Though this effort is far from being completely successful, there is evidence that it may sufficiently reduce the availability of alcohol to this age group to produce a reduction in alcohol-related fatal crashes. In the last two decades, the rate of alcohol-related traffic deaths for youth under age 21 has fallen from 22 per 100,000 in 1982 to 10 per 100,000 in 1996. During that period, alcohol use dropped from 70% to 50% among high school students and the number of binge drinkers (five or more drinks at a session) in that age group dropped from 40% to 30 %. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates that through 1996, 16,513 lives were saved by the minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) laws in the 50 states. The objective of this research was to determine the extent to which the decline in alcohol-related highway deaths among drivers under age 21 could be attributed to the MLDA and the zero tolerance (0.02 BAC limit for drivers under age 21) laws, which were based on the age-21 drinking limit.

Fatal crashes result from many factors that affect vehicle use in the United States. The status of the economy, the quality of vehicle and roadway systems, and alcohol sales and consumption among other factors may play a role in crash causation. Therefore, to study the impact of safety legislation, it was necessary to control for factors, other than these laws, that may have contributed to the observed changes in crash frequency. The procedure most frequently used to study the impact of legislation on crashes is to compare states with and without the laws of interest (see for example,[Hingson, Hereen, & Winter, 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b4-aam43_p265)[& 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b5-aam43_p265); [Johnson & Fell, 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b6-aam43_p265)). This approach depends upon selecting comparison states that are similar in significant characteristics to experimental states that have enacted the laws of interest. An alternative procedure is a panel study that would use all states over a substantial time. A state-by-year matrix can be created that would lend itself to regression analysis, where alcohol-related fatal crashes, alcohol-related fatalities, or drinking drivers in fatal crashes become the dependent variable, and alcohol safety laws and other factors known to influence fatal crashes become the independent predictor variables.

[Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265) presents a model of factors influencing crash causation that guided the present study. On the left-hand side of the diagram, Item 1 – _State Background Factors_ comprise those factors that previous studies have shown to have an effect on the total number of fatal crashes occurring in a state. Examples of such factors are the number of licensed drivers, the vehicle miles traveled, and the unemployment level. Item 2 – includes the MLDA and the zero tolerance laws that are the subjects of the present investigation. Item 3 is the criterion or outcome measure, the odds ratio formed by dividing the number of underage drinking drivers in fatal crashes by the number of nondrinking underage drivers in such crashes. Item 4 – state per capita alcohol consumption, Item 5 – general alcohol safety laws, and Item 6 – safety belt laws are significant factors hypothesized to impact the number of alcohol-related crashes in a state.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)STATE BACKGROUND FACTORS (Item 1, [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265))

The ratio of drinking to nondrinking drivers was used to minimize the effect of state environmental factors, such as urban versus rural composition, the number of licensed drivers in a state, the number of vehicle miles traveled in a state, and changes in vehicle safety (e.g., air bags) and roadway safety features, all of which were expected to influence the total number of fatal crashes, but not to have a differential effect on the proportion of alcohol-related crashes. In theory, unless the background factors on the left are correlated with alcohol-related crashes through an intermediate measure, such as alcohol consumption, they should not appear in the final predictor set.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)UNDERAGE CONSUMPTION AND DRINKING AND DRIVING LAWS (Item 2, [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265))

Some states have prohibited the sale of alcohol to individuals under the age of 21 since the repeal of Prohibition in the 1930s. However, between 1970 and 1975, 29 states lowered their drinking age to between 18 and 20. ([Toomey, Rosenfeld, & Wagenaar, 1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b13-aam43_p265)). This trend to lower the drinking age was reversed when research indicated that lower drinking ages were associated with increased alcohol-related fatalities among youth ([GAO, 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b2-aam43_p265)). By 1989, stimulated by federal legislation that penalized states not enacting age 21 drinking limit laws, all the US population was covered by MLDA laws (see [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#t1-aam43_p265)). The zero tolerance law, a companion to the MLDA law, was initially adopted by Maine in 1983 and, with support from federal legislation, in all 50 states by 1998. The zero tolerance laws provide that the blood alcohol concentration (BAC) limit for drivers under age 21 is .02, or essentially zero. [Hingson et al. (1994)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b4-aam43_p265) studied the first 12 states that adopted these laws and found a 20% decline in nighttime fatal crashes (a surrogate for alcohol-related crashes) as compared to similar states without such laws. The rate of adoption of this law over the 16 years of the current study is shown in [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#t1-aam43_p265).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)DEPENDENT VARIABLE; ODDS RATIO DRINKING TO NONDRINKING DRIVERS IN FATAL CRASHES (Item 3, [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265))

The Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) provides the number and BACs of drivers in fatal crashes. Beginning in 1982, data with comparable information on driver BACs are available for all 50 states. Each of the three crash measures can be related to impaired driving where the BAC of the driver is known. [Klein (1986)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b7-aam43_p265) has developed an imputation program for drivers whose BACs are not known. This imputation procedure uses the observed BAC values for the 73.3% of fatally injured drivers and the 25.3% of surviving drivers for which the BACs are known and provides a probability estimate for the remaining drivers. This imputation procedure assigns each case with an unknown BAC to one of three class intervals: BAC=0, BAC=.01 to .099, and BAC=.10 or greater. Using this estimation procedure, comparable BAC data were available for this study for all 50 states and the District of Columbia for 16 years (1982 to 1997).

Because the two laws—MLDA and zero tolerance—in this study affected only persons under the age of 21, only drivers age 20 and under in fatal crashes were included in the study. Further, since these laws were aimed at either reducing drinking or impaired driving, the number of drivers in fatal crashes who had been drinking (as indicated by a positive BAC) were ‘standardized’ by expressing their numbers relative to the number of nondrinking drivers in the same age group, whose numbers should not be affected by the law. Analyzing the log of this ratio, or odds, allows the resulting coefficient to be readily expressed as a percentage reduction or increase involvement by alcohol-positive drivers due to the factors entering into the study. Relating only drivers in fatal crashes with measurable BACs to drivers with no alcohol in their systems also assists in controlling for those factors that impact all fatal crashes but are not specifically related to impaired driving.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)STATE PER CAPITA ALCOHOL CONSUMPTION (Item 4, [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265))

Beer has been shown to be the beverage of choice for individuals convicted of driving while intoxicated (DWI) ([Berger & Snortum, 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b1-aam43_p265)). For the present study, separate state per capita consumption levels were available for wine, beer, and spirits ([Williams, Stinson, Sanchez, & Dufour, 1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b19-aam43_p265)). Only beer and total consumption, however, correlated significantly with the number of drinking drivers in fatal crashes, so beer emerged as the principal relevant measure of alcohol consumption. Separate per capita consumption measures for individuals under age 21 were not available, but overall state consumption was hypothesized to be potentially related to both alcohol-related crashes and the passage of alcohol-related control laws. High rates of alcohol-related problems could increase support for such legislation. On the other hand, high use rates could raise opposition to laws that threaten heavy drinkers. Alternatively, the passage of alcohol safety legislation could reduce consumption by deterring heavy drinking among those drinking away from their residence where they must drive to get home.

To determine the direction of this effect, two preliminary analyses were conducted. First, the annual beer consumption levels for states adopting .08 laws, before the law was adopted, were compared with states not adopting this legislation. The average per capita consumption for .08 states was 1.42 (+/− .04 se), and the mean for the non-.08 states was 1.40 (=/− .07 se) indicating that there was no significant difference (p=.826) between the two groups of states. Further, when the date of adoption of the .08 law was examined, the early adopters did not have different levels of per capita consumption (p=.311). A second study looked at the period following the enactment of .10, .08, and ALR laws in states adopting such legislation and compared it with the period leading up to the implementation of these laws. For all three laws, there was a reduction in beer consumption following enactment of the laws (.10 = −3.22%, .08 = −3.49%, ALR = −2.16%). All these differences were significant at p< .001. Thus, the evidence favors the hypothesis that any relationship between the safety laws and consumption is in the direction of the laws affecting consumption rather than the other way around.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)GENERAL ALCOHOL SAFETY LAWS (Item 5, [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265))

Laws making driving with at least a .10 BAC illegal limit have been enacted in all but two states. [Zador, Lund, Field, & Weinberg (1988)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b20-aam43_p265) found that illegal per se laws were associated with a 2% reduction in fatal crashes. In 17 states, this level has been lowered to .08. [Hingson and his coworkers (1996)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b5-aam43_p265) studied five states with and without .08 per se laws and found that these laws were associated with significant reductions in the number of alcohol-related crashes involving drivers with BACs at .08 or greater. The number of states with administrative license revocation (ALR) laws has increased from 3 to 40. ALR laws have been demonstrated to have a general deterrent effect as indicated by a reduction in alcohol-related crashes in studies by [Zador et al. (1988)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b20-aam43_p265) and [Klein (1989)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b8-aam43_p265). [Voas, Tippetts, and Taylor (1999, in-press)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b14-aam43_p265) studied all three alcohol safety laws in the 50 states and the District of Columbia over 16 years (from 1982 to 1997) and found that each law produced a significant reduction in the proportion of drinking drivers in fatal crashes. [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#t1-aam43_p265) shows the proportionate coverage of the US population for each of these laws from 1982 to 1997.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)SAFETY BELT LAWS (Item 6, [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265))

Occupant restraint programs include three types of laws: child safety seat laws and secondary and primary _safety belt laws_. Since this study focuses on alcohol use by drivers, child safety seat laws are not included. Secondary and primary safety belt laws are combined into a single three-level variable: 0, 1, and 2. This weights primary safety belt laws as twice as effective as secondary laws. This is probably reasonable since the passage of secondary laws raised wearing rates from approximately 30% to 60%, and primary laws where strongly enforced, such as in California, raised wearing rates in some localities to 90% ([Lange & Voas, 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b9-aam43_p265); [NHTSA, 1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b11-aam43_p265)). Attempts to use two separate variables to represent these laws were frustrated because some states moved directly to primary laws while others first passed secondary laws.

Using safety belts has a complex relationship to alcohol-related crashes. In the absence of a safety belt law, wearing rates were low and nondrinking drivers were more likely to wear their safety belts. At the low-wearing rates, safety belts primarily protected sober drivers. However, at relatively high-wearing rates, the proportion of nonwearers among sober drivers is relatively small, and the proportion of nonwearers among drinking drivers is relatively high. Thus, additional increases in wearing rates provide a greater relative protection to drinking drivers. In this study, safety belt laws were hypothesized to reduce the proportion of drinking drivers in fatal crashes. Initially, sober drivers were more likely to wear safety belts than were drinking drivers. However, once wearing rates were high (60% to 70% in secondary law states), these additional increases produced by primary laws (up to 90% wearing rates) had a greater effect on drinking drivers. This effect was demonstrated in a study by [Lange and Voas (1998)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b9-aam43_p265) of the implementation of a primary safety belt law in California. Therefore, a law encouraging the wearing of safety belts will more greatly affect the low-wearing rates of the drinking drivers (the numerator) than nondrinking drivers who already have a higher usage rate (the denominator). Thus, we expected this factor to show a negative relationship to the ratio of impaired drivers in fatal crashes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)ANALYSIS

For an evaluation of the effects of MLDA and zero tolerance laws, we analyzed FARS data using weighted least squares (WLS) regression models in which the ratios of alcohol-involved drivers to non-alcohol-involved drivers were aggregated into a set of state-by-year data points—that is, varying by state and, within state, by year. Using this ratio, alcohol-related drivers relative to non-alcohol-related drivers served to control for general driving and safety trends (reducing the need for covariates that predict fatal crashes) and also to control for differences among states in sheer size. Further, this odds ratio was transformed using a natural log to make the coefficients for the laws’ effects readily interpretable in terms of the percentage of increase or decrease. (Incidentally, this transformation also improves the normality of the distribution of the dependent variable, making statistical assumptions for parametric procedures more tenable).

For each of the 16 years, two sums were aggregated: the number of drivers measured or imputed to be alcohol-positive and the number of drivers measured or imputed to be alcohol-negative. Drivers not having a measured BAC had an imputed probability of being alcohol-positive and another imputed probability of being alcohol-negative; for these drivers, the probabilities were used as fractional case weights in the aggregation process.

### WEIGHTING

We used WLS regression models, weighting the cases for some states more than others, because the data for the more populous states were generally more stable (i.e., contained less sampling error) than the data from smaller states. This occurs because, in a large state, the total pool of crash-involved drivers in any given year (or month) represents a much larger sample and, therefore, will be less susceptible to fluctuation resulting from random factors. In a smaller state, the difference of one or two cases per month can produce large differences in a ratio.

Case weights were determined by using bootstrap resampling procedures to estimate the sampling variability within each state per year. Within-state variability is largely caused by the sampling size of the state’s pool of crashes and, therefore, taps into the size-of-state dimension very well (Spearman’s rho=.858). In addition, the weighting derived from within-state variability has the desirable qualities of a narrower range and a less extreme distribution. Larger states have lower resampling variability because they have more crash-involved drivers. Thus, random fluctuations tend to wash out, thereby providing more stable and reliable ratios. Weighting cases by this measure naturally places more importance on the experience of larger states or at least on states having a larger traffic problem in terms of numbers of fatal crashes. These case weights had a mean of 1.0 across all 51 states within each period, ranging from a low of approximately 0.25 (North Dakota, Alaska, and Rhode Island) to slightly greater than 2.5 (California).

### INDEPENDENT VARIABLES/COVARIATES

To appropriately estimate the size of changes attributable to the two laws of primary interest, we included other alcohol-related laws in the model to apportion out their effects as well. Those included were ALR laws, .10 and .08 per se limit laws (with a per se level of greater than .10 considered the same as absence of a per se law), and safety belt laws.

These laws were generally modeled as dichotomous dummy variables; but, when a law became effective partway through a year, the variable represented the proportion of the period during which the law was in effect. Additionally, for the zero tolerance and MLDA laws, states often began by having laws affecting limited portions of the youth population (e.g., only applied to those under age 18 instead of all those under age 21). In these situations, the dummy represented the proportion of the state’s youth population affected by the law in that year as determined by the age representation of non-alcohol-involved drivers in fatal crashes in that state during that year. Safety restraint laws were modeled as a single two-step variable, with a secondary law represented with a value of 0.5 and a primary law represented by 1.0.

To avoid overfitting a model with a dummy parameter for each state and to explain variation over time within states, other variables relating to states’ environments and conditions were used as covariates (Items 1, 4, 5, and 6 in [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#f1-aam43_p265)). The most important of these was per capita beer consumption (at least in terms of correlating the prevalence of alcohol in drivers involved in fatal crashes). Consumption data were not available for 1996 and 1997, the 2 years during which many of these laws were passed. Therefore, we decided to use an average beer consumption level, constant over time within state, rather than eliminating one of the strongest predictors of alcohol-involved crashes. However, because it has been argued that the laws impact traffic safety indirectly via reduction in alcohol consumption, the two preliminary analyses described above were performed to determine the effects of the laws on beer and other alcohol consumption. These analyses factored out between-state differences, so that the effect tested would represent within-state change due to the laws. This avoided the possibility of wrongly confounding the laws’ effect on consumption with the possible consumption levels effect on whether a state would pass an alcohol safety law. When we found small, but significant, effects, we adjusted these state consumption levels for the effects of the laws in those states passing the laws. As such, the beer consumption variable served as a between-state covariate only, remaining constant over time within the state.

Among the other variables that vary both between-states within the same period and within-states over time, three were found to be important predictors: the average vehicle miles traveled (VMT) per licensed driver, the urban and rural distribution of the state’s population, and the unemployment rates. The two components of the VMT per driver—total state VMT and number of licensed drivers—were also available for use in the model. However, since our dependent variable is a rate and, therefore, already standardized by state size (by dividing by the number of alcohol-negative drivers in that state), the nonsignificance of these measures was anticipated.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)RESULTS

The results of this analysis are provided in [Table 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#t2-aam43_p265). As we expected with one exception, the state background variables were not related to the impaired driver odds ratio. There was, however, a significant negative relationship between vehicle miles of driving exposure per licensed driver and probability of having a positive BAC when the fatal crash occurred. This finding is contrary to those studies of the relationship of VMT to alcohol-related crashes. Because discretionary driving travel, which is more likely to involve drinking drivers, increases more rapidly, alcohol-related crashes increase with increasing VMT. However, changes in VMT are normally associated with economic expansions and recessions that effect discretionary driving. In the present case, economic factors were controlled by the inclusion of the unemployment index. Further, the VMT measure was only available for all groups where the dependent measure drinking drivers in fatal crashes included only those under age 21. Therefore, this relationship is difficult to interpret. The adjusted beer consumption measure was, as expected, positively correlated with the impaired driver odds ratio indicating that states with higher consumption levels had more impaired underage drivers. States with safety belt legislation had proportionately fewer positive BAC drivers under age 21 in fatal crashes suggesting that safety belt laws have a greater effect on the behavior of drinking than nondrinking youthful drivers.

Particularly striking are the substantial effect sizes for the MLDA and zero tolerance laws targeted at this age group. The zero tolerance effect appears larger in this analysis. This may be because two-thirds of the states had already adopted MLDA laws by 1982 when this study began. Two of the three general drinking-and-driving laws that affect drivers of all ages also showed significant effect sizes for underage drivers. The coefficient for the .08 law represented a 6% decline in drinking drivers in fatal crashes, but this effect size was not statistically significant.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235)DISCUSSION

The present study is not the first to produce evidence for the effectiveness of MLDA and zero tolerance laws. However, the present study covers the longest period (16 years) and more states (50, plus the District of Columbia) than most previous studies. It also specifically includes potential confounding variables such as alcohol consumption and safety belt laws not directly considered in most previous studies. The credibility of the results is strengthened by their conformity to theoretical expectations—beer consumption is associated with higher rates of drinking drivers involved in fatal crashes, whereas safety belt laws are correlated with lower rates of drinking drivers involved in fatal crashes. Further, the relationship between alcohol safety laws and reductions in drinking drivers involved in crashes, though significant, are modest and generally consistent with the results of other studies. [Williams, Rich, Zador, and Robertson (1974)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b18-aam43_p265) found a 28% reduction in fatal crashes among 15- to 20-year olds following the enactment of MLDA laws for the affected age groups, and [Wagenaar (1993)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b15-aam43_p265) found a 20% reduction attributable to the MLDA. [Hingson et al. (1994)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b4-aam43_p265) found a 20% reduction in single-vehicle nighttime crashes for drivers, ages 15 to 20, in states passing zero tolerance laws.

Using the ratio of drinking to nondrinking drivers in fatal crashes is also a strength as it minimizes the potential impact of factors that may influence the total number of fatal crashes but not the proportion that are alcohol related. In addition to such factors, which were previously noted, there was a change in the size of the 15- to 20-age youth cohort in the United States. (During the years covered by this study, there was an initial decline of 10% in the total numbers in the 15-to 20-age group followed by an increase of 7% in the last 4 years.) The use of the ratio minimizes the potential for these changes in the size of the youth cohort to affect the results of the current study.

Though this study has a number of strengths, it has a weakness inherent in all regression analyses. It is sensitive to specification effects. The validity relies on the extent to which all significant predictors of the dependent variable have been accounted for in the analysis. In the present case, the national norms regarding drinking and driving may have changed, which is an underlying factor in both the passage of alcohol safety legislation and the number of drinking drivers involved in fatal crashes. There is strong evidence that such a normative change has occurred since 1980. This is about the time when several citizen activist groups—for example, Remove Intoxicated Drivers (RID), Mothers Against Drunk Driving (MADD), Students Against Drunk Drivers (SADD)—were founded ([McCarthy & Harvey, 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b10-aam43_p265)). Increased activism and research interest by local, state, and federal governments led to a large increase in press coverage of the drinking-and-driving issue and a flood of new alcohol safety legislation. This study did not include any measure of media coverage of the drinking-and-driving issue or any measure of public attitudes toward drinking and driving since such a measure was not available by year and state during the period covered by this study. Possibly, the public’s attention to the drinking-and-driving issue is producing both the types of laws and the reduction in drinking drivers in fatal crashes. The greater reduction in percentage of alcohol-related fatalities among youth under age 21 (compared to adults) over the 16 years from 1982 to 1996 ([NHTSA, 1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b12-aam43_p265)) suggests that more than public attention to the drinking-and-driving issue is affecting underage drinking drivers. However, it has generally been found that media campaigns in the absence of newly institutionalized actions (such as legislation) do not produce measurable reductions in crash frequencies ([Wilde, Hoste, Sheppard, & Wind, 1971](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b17-aam43_p265)).

Overall, the results of this study suggest that the policy of limiting youth access to alcohol through MLDA laws and reinforcing this action by making it illegal for underage drivers to have any alcohol in their system when driving is reducing the proportion of fatal crashes involving drinking drivers. This effect is in addition to the impact of the more general drinking-and-driving laws. It is not surprising that the effect of the general .08 per se law, though in the right direction, was not significant for underage drivers given that their effective limit under the zero tolerance law is a BAC of .02.

The effects of these individual laws cannot be completely separated. All of these laws are operating in a larger context in which public attitudes towards drinking and driving are influencing both the passage of safety legislation and the occurrence of fatal crashes. Safety laws, in turn, serve to publicize the limits of normative behavior. The effect sizes obtained for the laws in this study undoubtedly reflect influences beyond those resulting from their enforcement. There is evidence that the MLDA laws are only weakly enforced ([Wagenaar & Wolfson, 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235#b16-aam43_p265)); nevertheless, they apparently have had a significant effect on the reduction in alcohol-related fatal crashes involving underage drivers. This suggests that normative changes in drinking and in drinking and driving are occurring that are influenced by the existence of the legislation independently of the strength of its enforcement.

args.summary:
This is a 1999 research article published in the Annual Proceedings of the Association for the Advancement of Automotive Medicine, authored by Voas, Tippetts, and Fell. The study evaluates the effectiveness of US laws limiting youth drinking — specifically Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA) laws (age 21) and zero tolerance laws (0.02 BAC limit for drivers under 21) — in reducing alcohol-related fatal crash involvements among drivers under age 21.

Using data from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) from 1982 to 1997 across all 50 states and DC, the researchers conducted a pooled cross-sectional time-series analysis using weighted least squares regression. The dependent variable was the odds ratio of drinking to non-drinking drivers under age 21 in fatal crashes. Key covariates included per capita beer consumption, vehicle miles traveled, unemployment rates, and other alcohol safety laws (per se .10 and .08 BAC laws, administrative license revocation, safety belt laws).

Key findings:
- The MLDA law was associated with an 18.9% reduction in the proportion of underage drinking drivers in fatal crashes.
- The zero tolerance law was associated with a 24.4% reduction.
- Per se .10 laws reduced underage drinking drivers by 17.8%, administrative license revocation by 19.0%, and safety belt laws by 20.6%.
- The .08 per se law showed a non-significant 6.4% reduction for underage drivers.
- Beer consumption was positively correlated with impaired underage drivers; safety belt laws were negatively correlated.

The study notes that alcohol-related traffic deaths for youth under 21 fell from 22 per 100,000 in 1982 to 10 per 100,000 in 1996. NHTSA estimated that through 1996, 16,513 lives were saved by MLDA laws. The authors acknowledge limitations, including potential confounding from changing public attitudes toward drinking and driving and the inability to fully separate the effects of individual laws from broader normative shifts.

# Why A Minimum Legal Drinking Age of 21 Works

## Key points

![A sign that says, "Notice: No drinking under 21."](/alcohol/images/fact-sheets/No-drinking-under-age-21.jpg "no-drinking-under-21")

## Minimum legal drinking age laws

## Health impacts

### Setting the legal age to 21 for buying alcohol has helped protect health by:

#### Fewer motor vehicle crashes

Before the national law was in place, states that raised their MLDA to 21 years had a 16% drop in motor vehicle crashes.[2](#cdcreference_2)

#### Less underage drinking

After states raised their MLDA to 21 years in 1984, the percentage of people who drank before turning 21 went down.

Young adults also drank less alcohol when states raised their MLDA.

### Did you know?

By following the MLDA laws, communities can reduce underage drinking. Learn more about [underage drinking](/alcohol/underage-drinking/index.html) and how you [can help prevent it](/alcohol/underage-drinking/community-strategies.html#cdc_health_safety_special_topic_types-proven-community-strategies-to-reduce-underage-drinking).

#### Safer, healthier people and communities

The MLDA of 21 years helps lower the risk of developing alcohol and other substance use disorders, for those who drink alcohol. It also supports families and communities by leading to fewer harmful births, lower rates of suicide and homicide, and fewer deaths from alcohol poisoning.

## Spotlight

Several national organizations have indicated support for the MLDA of age 21:

Why is 21 the Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA)?

More than 25,000 lives have been saved in the U.S. thanks to the MLDA. This law continues to curb teen drinking and prevent tragedies—decreasing crashes by an estimated 16 percent and keeping young people safe.

Why do we make young people wait until 21 to drink alcohol?

Many activities have ages of initiation. A person must wait until age 16 to start driving, age 18 to marry without parental consent, age 35 to become president and so on.

The age limit for alcohol is based on research which shows that young people react differently to alcohol. Teens get drunk twice as fast as adults, 9 but have more trouble knowing when to stop. Teens naturally overdo it and binge more often than adults.

 

Enforcing the legal drinking age of 21 reduces traffic crashes involving drunk teens, 4-6 protects young people’s maturing brains,12,14 and keeps young people safer overall.

Zeigler DW, Wang CC, Yoast RA, Dickinson BD, Mccaffree MA, Robinowitz CB, et al. The Neurocognitive Effects of Alcohol on Adolescents and College Students. Prev Med 2005 Jan;40(1):23-32.  [Read More](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15530577)

How many children under the age of 12 try marijuana each day in the U.S.?

Children as young as nine years old already start viewing alcohol in a more positive way, and approximately 3,300 kids as young as 12 try marijuana each day.

What percentage of teens have tried alcohol? +

About 30 percent of 8th graders have tried alcohol.   
 

###### References Johnston, L. D., Miech, R. A., O’Malley, P. M., Bachman, J. G., Schulenberg, J. E., & Patrick, M. E. (2020). Monitoring the Future national survey results on drug use 1975-2019: Overview, key findings on adolescent drug use. Ann Arbor: Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan.

How does underage drinking affect teens as they get older?

Youth who start drinking before age 15 years are six times more likely to develop alcohol dependence or abuse later in life than those who begin drinking at or after age 21 years.

References  
Center for Behavioral Health Statistics and Quality. 2015 National Survey on Drug Use and Health: Detailed Tables. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Rockville, MD; 2016.

How many people become addicted to cannabis?

About 1 in 10 cannabis users will become addicted. For people who begin using before the   age of 18, that number rises to 1 in 6.   

###### References Lopez-Quintero, C, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC). Drug Alcohol Depend. 115(1-2): p. 120-30

How common is it that kids drink and do drugs?

1 in 3 youth who drink alcohol have also combined alcohol with cannabis on the same evenings. On these occasions, they tend to experience 2-3 times more problems compared to those when they only consume alcohol.    

###### References Mallett, K.A., Turrisi, R., Hultgren, B.A., Sell, N., Reavy, R., & Cleveland, M. (2017). When alcohol is only part of the problem: An event-level analysis of negative consequences related to alcohol and other substance use. Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, 31(3), 307-314. PMCID: PMC5422123.

Would lowering the legal drinking age make alcohol less of a big deal, and less attractive to teens?

History says no. When states had lower legal drinking ages in the U.S., the underage drinking problem was worse.3 For example, before the 21 minimum legal drinking age was implemented by all states, teens drinking and driving were involved in over twice as many fatal traffic crashes as today.3  References  
3. Fell, James. From “Chapter 2: Federalism: Resolved, the Federal Government should restore each State’s freedom to set its drinking age.” in Ellis, Richard and Nelson, Michael (eds.) Debating Reform. CQPress Publishers, Fall 2009.

Can’t parents teach their teens how to drink alcohol responsibly by giving them small amounts-under supervision-before they reach 21?

Some states permit parents to do this with their own child (rarely, if ever, with someone else’s child), but there’s no evidence that this approach actually works.3 As matter of fact, there is evidence to contrary. When teens feel they have their parents’ approval to drink, they do it more and more often when they are not with their parents. When parents have concrete, enforced rules about alcohol, according to binge drinking statistics, young people binge drink less. However, kids who are simply more connected with their parents, for example, who attend family dinners more frequently, are less likely to drink alcohol or use other drugs among other risk factors.7

History of the Minimum Legal Drinking Age Act

On July 17, 1984, President Ronald Reagan signed the Minimum Legal Drinking Age-21 Law, alongside drunk driving victims and survivors from MADD, then-U.S. Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole, and Congressional sponsors. Over the last four decades, this landmark federal law has served as a blueprint for MADD’s efforts to end impaired driving.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates approximately 800 to 900 lives are saved every year as a result of setting the minimum legal drinking age in the U.S. at 21.

![President Ronald Reagan signs the Minimum Legal Drinking Age-21 Law, alongside drunk driving victims and survivors from MADD, then-U.S. Transportation Secretary Elizabeth Dole, and Congressional sponsors](https://madd.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/ReganSigning-2.png)

Myth & Facts

There are many unfortunate and dangerous myths when it comes to underage use of alcohol and other drugs. Click on each myth below to learn the truth and the facts that support it.

MYTH: MADD is working to eliminate teen drunk driving rather than focusing on underage drinking prevention efforts.

False. One of MADD’s pillars is promoting zero tolerance for underage drinking.

Kids who start drinking young are seven times more likely to be in an alcohol-related crash according to underage drinking statistics. MADD knows that by preventing underage drinking today, we can end drunk driving tomorrow. 

###### 

##### References  Hingson, Ralph, et al. “Age of Drinking Onset, Driving After Drinking, and Involvement in Alcohol-Related Motor Vehicle Crashes.” DOT HS 809 188. Washington, DC: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, January 2001. [Read More](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11789578/)

MYTH: Europeans let their kids drink at an early age, yet they do not have the alcohol-related problems we do.

Actually, in Europe, young people have higher intoxication rates than in the United States, and less than a quarter had lower or equivalent rates to the United States. Also, a greater percentage of young people in the majority of Europe report binge drinking at higher rates than compared to their US counterparts.1-2Most European youth have higher rates of alcohol-related problems because of their heavy drinking. 

 

Perhaps the best example of fact versus myth is what happened in New Zealand. In 1999, New Zealand lowered its purchase age from 20 to 18. Not only did drunk driving crashes increase, but youth started to drink earlier, binge drinking escalated, and in the 12 months following the decrease in legal drinking age, there was a 50 percent increase in drunk teens, 18- and 19-year-old patients, at the Auckland Hospital emergency room.3

##### References 1. The ESPAD Report 2003.  Alcohol and Other Drug Use Among Students in 35 European Countries.  Published 2004. [Read excerpts here.](http://www.monitoringthefuture.org/pubs/espadusa2003.pdf) 2. Johnston, L. D., O’Malley, P. M., Bachman, J. G., & Schulenberg, J. E. (2004). Monitoring the Future national results on adolescent drug use: Overview of key findings, 2003 (NIH Publication No. 04-5506). Bethesda, MD: National Institute on Drug Abuse. [Read the overview here. 3. Kyrpi, Kypros, et al.  “Minimum Purchasing Age for Alcohol and Traffic Crash Injuries Among 15- to 19-Year-Olds in New Zealand.” American Journal of Public Health, January 2006, Voi 96, No. 1.](http://www.monitoringthefuture.org/pubs/monographs/overview2003.pdf) [Read the study here.](https://d.docs.live.net/192d19f37903f1eb/Freelance/MADD/Read%20the%20study%20here.)

MYTH: Alcohol is not that big of a deal anymore. Shouldn’t I be more worried about other more dangerous drugs?

Teen alcohol use kills 4,300 people each year—that’s more than all illegal drugs combined.   

##### References Sacks JJ, Gonzales KR, Bouchery EE, Tomedi LE, Brewer RD. 2010 National and State Costs of Excessive Alcohol Consumption. Am J Prev Med 2015; 49(5):e73–e79. [Read More](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26477807/)

MYTH: The law only makes youth want to drink because it’s a “forbidden fruit.”

When the “forbidden fruit” is no longer forbidden, youth simply drink more. In states where the drinking age was 18, teens statistically drank more than in states where the minimum drinking age was 21. They continued to drink more as adults in their early 20s.4 

 

##### References 4. Maisto, S.A., & Rachal, J.V. (1980). Indications of the relationship between adolescent drinking practices, related behaviors, and drinking age law: An examination of data from a national sample. In H. Wechsler (Ed.), Minimum drinking age laws: An evaluation (pp.155-176). Lexington, MA: D.C. Heath & Co. [Read More](https://trid.trb.org/view/192473)

MYTH: Lowering the drinking age will encourage young people to be responsible consumers rather than drink at uncontrolled, private parties.

Many youth drink with the goal to get drunk. They are not “wired” in the brain to assess risk and to be responsible when it comes to risky behavior. There is no class or situation that will prompt a teen to drink responsibly when alcohol flows freely.

MYTH: Drinking is just a phase all kids go through; they’ll grow out of it.

Actually, many don’t. In fact, the earlier someone begins drinking, the more likely they are to be alcohol dependent in later life. More than 40 percent of individuals who start drinking before the age of 13 will develop alcohol abuse or alcohol dependence at some point in their lives.5 Ninety-five percent of the 14 million people who are alcohol dependent began drinking before the legal age of 21.6 

 

##### References 5. Grant, Bridgett and Deborah Dawson. “Age at Onset of Alcohol Use and Its Association with DSM-IV Alcohol Abuse and Dependence.” Results from the National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey.  Journal of Substance Abuse 9 (1997): 103-110. 6. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. “Alcohol Dependence or Abuse and Age at First Use.” Washington, DC: Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Applied Studies, October 22, 2004. [Read the full study here](http://www.oas.samhsa.gov/2k4/ageDepedence/ageDependence.htm)[.](http://www.oas.samhsa.gov/2k4/ageDepedence/ageDependence.htm)

MYTH: If I’m old enough to go to war, I should be old enough to drink.

21 is the minimum age because a person’s brain does not stop developing until his or her early to mid-20s. Drinking alcohol while the brain is still developing can lead to long-lasting deficits in cognitive abilities, including learning and memory. 

 

Alcohol use by those under 21 is also related to numerous health problems including injuries and death resulting from alcohol poisoning, car crashes, suicide, homicide, assaults, drowning, and recreational mishaps. Not to mention that the early onset of drinking by youth significantly increases the risk of future health problems such as addiction. 

 

Regardless of a person’s profession, underage drinking is still dangerous and unsafe. It is a fact based on biology not maturity or service to our country. 

 

##### References  How alcohol affects brain: <https://pubs.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/aa63/aa63.htm>   Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. “Alcohol Dependence or Abuse and Age at First Use.” Washington, DC: Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Applied Studies, October 22, 2004. [Read the full study here](http://www.oas.samhsa.gov/2k4/ageDepedence/ageDependence.htm)[.](http://www.oas.samhsa.gov/2k4/ageDepedence/ageDependence.htm)

MYTH: MADD says kids shouldn’t have access to marijuana, but marijuana isn’t as bad as alcohol, I mean at least it is not addictive.

Marijuana is very addictive! In fact, in 2016 over 4 million people were diagnosed with substance use disorder due to marijuana use. Marijuana that is produced and sold not has a much higher content of THC than what was seen on the market in the 60’s and 70’s. Just like with alcohol, the young brain is not ready to protect teens against drugs like marijuana. 

 

##### References  Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. (2017). Key substance use and mental health indicators in the United States: Results from the 2016 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (HHS Publication No. SMA 17-5044, NSDUH Series H-52). People who start drinking or doing drugs at an early age can face severe, persistent problems throughout their lives. Whether you are a parent or a teen, you have the power to make a difference.

# Minimum Legal Drinking Age 21 Laws

The primary strategy to reduce underage drinking, as well as drinking and driving, has been restricting access to alcohol via minimum purchase age laws. Since July 1988 the minimum legal drinking age has been 21 in all States. There is strong evidence that MLDA-21 laws reduce drinking, driving after drinking, and alcohol-related crashes and injuries among youth (McCartt, Hellinga, & Kirley, 2010; Shults et al., 2001; Wagenaar & Toomey, 2002). In fact, MLDA-21 laws reduced youth drinking and driving more than youth drinking alone (using the measurements of self-reporting and testing of impaired drivers in fatal crashes) (McCartt, Hellinga, & Kirley, 2010). Drinking and driving has become less socially acceptable among youth, and more youth have separated their drinking from their driving (Hedlund et al., 2001).

MLDA-21 law enforcement can take several forms:

Fell et al. (2016) found that nine laws that support enforcement of the MLDA-21 law significantly decreased fatal crash ratios of drinking to nondrinking drivers under 21. The laws are: (1) possession of alcohol, (2) purchase of alcohol, (3) use alcohol and lose your license, (4) zero-tolerance .02 BAC limit for underage, (5) age of bartender as 21 or older, (6) State responsible beverage service program, (7) fake identification support provisions for retailers, (8) dram shop liability, and (9) social host civil liability. The study estimated that combined, the nine MLDA-21 support laws save approximately 1,355 lives each year; however, only 5 States have enacted all nine laws. While these enforcement strategies have been used frequently, few have been evaluated.

The implementation of MLDA-21 laws for alcohol vendors, adults, and youth differs substantially from State to State. See the Alcohol Policy Information System for State-by-State summaries of some of the key provisions (APIS, 2021).

**Use:**

The minimum age to purchase alcohol is 21 years old in all 50 States and the District of Columbia.

**Effectiveness:**

Several reviews point to the effectiveness of MLDA-21 laws. Shults et al. (2001) identified 33 published studies examining the effects of changing the legal drinking age. Overall, changes to the MLDA affected alcohol-related crashes by 10% to 16%, with crashes decreasing when the MLDA was raised, and increasing when it was lowered. Wagenaar and Toomey (2002) reviewed 79 high-quality studies examining the relationship between the MLDA and crashes. Of these studies, 58% found fewer crashes associated with a higher MLDA, whereas none found fewer crashes associated with a lower MLDA. These findings prompted McCartt, Hellinga, and Kirley (2010) to conclude: “The highway safety benefits of MLDA-21 have been proven, and the cause-and-effect relationship between MLDA and highway crashes is clear. Deaths go up when the drinking age is lowered, and they go down when it is raised” (p. 180). NHTSA estimates that MLDA-21 laws have saved 31,959 lives since 1975 and an estimated 538 lives in 2017 alone (NCSA, 2019, 2022).

**Costs:**

Costs may be associated with training needed for enforcement of MLDA-21 laws. (See Countermeasures on Zero Tolerance Law Enforcement and Alcohol Vender Compliance Checks.)

#### **Time to implement:**

MLDA-21 laws can be implemented as soon as appropriate legislation is enacted.

This webpage from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) discusses the Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA) of 21 in the United States. Since July 1988, the MLDA has been 21 in all states. Strong evidence shows that MLDA-21 laws reduce drinking, driving after drinking, and alcohol-related crashes and injuries among youth. The laws have made drinking and driving less socially acceptable among young people.

Fell et al. (2016) identified nine laws that support MLDA-21 enforcement and significantly decrease fatal crash ratios for drivers under 21: (1) possession of alcohol, (2) purchase of alcohol, (3) use alcohol and lose your license, (4) zero-tolerance .02 BAC limit for underage, (5) age of bartender as 21 or older, (6) State responsible beverage service program, (7) fake identification support provisions for retailers, (8) dram shop liability, and (9) social host civil liability. Combined, these laws save approximately 1,355 lives each year, though only 5 states have enacted all nine.

**Effectiveness:** Shults et al. (2001) reviewed 33 studies finding that MLDA changes affected alcohol-related crashes by 10% to 16%, with crashes decreasing when the MLDA was raised and increasing when lowered. Wagenaar and Toomey (2002) reviewed 79 studies, with 58% finding fewer crashes associated with a higher MLDA, and none finding fewer crashes with a lower MLDA. NHTSA estimates MLDA-21 laws have saved 31,959 lives since 1975 and an estimated 538 lives in 2017 alone.

**Implementation:** MLDA-21 laws can be implemented as soon as appropriate legislation is enacted. Costs may be associated with training for enforcement.
