## Prevalence of Lifetime Drinking

According to the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 12.7 million people ages 12 to 20 (32.9% in this age group) reported that they have had at least one drink in their lives.1,2 This includes:

* 6.2 million males ages 12 to 20 (31.4% in this age group)1,2
* 6.5 million females ages 12 to 20 (34.4% in this age group)1,2
* 80,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 to 20 (29.9% in this age group)1,2
* 427,000 Asian people ages 12 to 20 (17.5% in this age group)1,2
* 1.4 million Black or African American people ages 12 to 20 (27.3% in this age group)1,2
* 6.8 million White people ages 12 to 20 (36.3% in this age group)1,2
* 491,000 people of two or more races ages 12 to 20 (34.0% in this age group)1,2
* 3.4 million Hispanic or Latino people ages 12 to 20 (33.1% in this age group)1,2
* Estimates for Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people ages 12 to 20 were not presented because they were based on a relatively small number of respondents or had a large margin of error.1,2

## Prevalence of Past-Year Drinking

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 10.4 million people ages 12 to 20 (27.0% in this age group) reported that they drank in the past year.1,2 This includes:

* 5.1 million males ages 12 to 20 (25.7% in this age group)1,2
* 5.3 million females ages 12 to 20 (28.4% in this age group)1,2
* 58,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 to 20 (21.9% in this age group)1,2
* 360,000 Asian people ages 12 to 20 (14.7% in this age group)1,2
* 1.1 million Black or African American people ages 12 to 20 (21.4% in this age group)1,2
* 5.6 million White people ages 12 to 20 (30.2% in this age group)1,2
* 364,000 people of two or more races ages 12 to 20 (25.2% in this age group)1,2
* 2.8 million Hispanic or Latino people ages 12 to 20 (27.6% in this age group)1,2
* Estimates for Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people ages 12 to 20 were not presented because they were based on a relatively small number of respondents or had a large margin of error.1,2

## Prevalence of Past-Month Drinking

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 5.1 million people ages 12 to 20 (13.3% in this age group) reported that they drank in the past month.1,2 This includes:

* 2.4 million males ages 12 to 20 (12.4% in this age group)1,2
* 2.7 million females ages 12 to 20 (14.3% in this age group)1,2
* 22,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 to 20 (8.1% in this age group)1,2
* 172,000 Asian people ages 12 to 20 (7.0% in this age group)1,2
* 459,000 Black or African American people ages 12 to 20 (8.7% in this age group)1,2
* 7,000 Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people ages 12 to 20 (4.9% in this age group)1,2
* 3.0 million White people ages 12 to 20 (16.3% in this age group)1,2
* 188,000 people of two or more races ages 12 to 20 (13.0% in this age group)1,2
* 1.2 million Hispanic or Latino people ages 12 to 20 (12.1% in this age group)1,2

## Prevalence of Past-Month Binge Drinking

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 2.9 million people ages 12 to 20 (7.6% in this age group) reported binge drinking in the past month ([see glossary](/alcohols-effects-health/alcohol-topics-z/alcohol-facts-and-statistics/glossary "Glossary") for definition of binge drinking).1,2 This includes:

* 1.4 million males ages 12 to 20 (7.1% in this age group)1,2
* 1.6 million females ages 12 to 20 (8.3% in this age group)1,2
* 11,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 to 20 (4.2% in this age group)1,2
* 88,000 Asian people ages 12 to 20 (3.6% in this age group)1,2
* 289,000 Black or African American people ages 12 to 20 (5.5% in this age group)1,2
* 4,000 Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people ages 12 to 20 (2.9% in this age group)1,2
* 1.8 million White people ages 12 to 20 (9.6% in this age group)1,2
* 100,000 people of two or more races ages 12 to 20 (6.9% in this age group)1,2
* 665,000 Hispanic or Latino people ages 12 to 20 (6.5% in this age group)1,2

## Prevalence of Past-Month Heavy Alcohol Use

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 576,000 people ages 12 to 20 (1.5% in this age group) reported heavy alcohol use in the past month ([see glossary](/alcohols-effects-health/alcohol-topics-z/alcohol-facts-and-statistics/glossary "Glossary") for definition of heavy alcohol use).1,2 This includes:

* 320,000 males ages 12 to 20 (1.6% in this age group)1,2
* 256,000 females ages 12 to 20 (1.4% in this age group)1,2
* 3,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 to 20 (1.0% in this age group)1,2
* 2,000 Asian people ages 12 to 20 (0.1% in this age group)1,2
* 44,000 Black or African American people ages 12 to 20 (0.8% in this age group)1,2
* 383,000 White people ages 12 to 20 (2.1% in this age group)1,2
* 18,000 people of two or more races ages 12 to 20 (1.3% in this age group)1,2
* 123,000 Hispanic or Latino people ages 12 to 20 (1.2% in this age group)1,2
* Estimates for Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people ages 12 to 20 were not presented because they were based on a relatively small number of respondents or had a large margin of error.1,2

## Prevalence of High-Intensity Drinking

According to the 2024 Monitoring the Future survey, 3.0% of students in 12th grade reported high-intensity drinking (10+drinks in a row) in the last two weeks.3

## Consequences of Underage Alcohol Use

* [Underage drinking](https://www.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/brochures-and-fact-sheets/underage-drinking) contributes to a range of immediate and lasting consequences, such as injuries,4 sexual assaults,5 alcohol overdoses, and death.
* Alcohol is a factor in the deaths of thousands of people younger than age 21 in the United States each year. This includes:
  + 1,392 from motor vehicle crashes involving an alcohol-impaired driver (defined as having a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08 grams per deciliter) 6
  + 978 from homicides7
  + 644 from alcohol-related poisoning (overdose), fall injuries, fire injuries, and drowning7
  + 615 from suicides7

Please see the 2024 NSDUH [Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/data-we-collect/nsduh-national-survey-drug-use-and-health/national-releases/2024) and Section 2.3.4 of the [2024 Methodological Summary and Definitions Report](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2024-methodological-summary-and-definitions) for more details.

This webpage from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) provides comprehensive statistics on underage drinking in the United States (ages 12-20), updated August 2025, based primarily on the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH) and the 2024 Monitoring the Future survey.

**Key Statistics:**

- **Lifetime drinking:** 12.7 million (32.9%) of people ages 12-20 have had at least one drink.
- **Past-year drinking:** 10.4 million (27.0%) drank in the past year.
- **Past-month drinking:** 5.1 million (13.3%) drank in the past month.
- **Past-month binge drinking:** 2.9 million (7.6%) reported binge drinking.
- **Past-month heavy alcohol use:** 576,000 (1.5%) reported heavy alcohol use.
- **High-intensity drinking:** 3.0% of 12th graders reported drinking 10+ drinks in a row in the last two weeks.

**Demographic breakdowns** are provided by sex and race/ethnicity. Females generally had higher rates than males across most categories. By race, White youth had the highest prevalence rates across all categories, while Asian youth had the lowest.

**Consequences of underage alcohol use:** Alcohol is a factor in thousands of deaths annually among those under 21, including 1,392 from motor vehicle crashes involving an alcohol-impaired driver, 978 from homicides, 644 from alcohol-related poisoning, fall injuries, fire injuries, and drowning, and 615 from suicides.

The page notes that 2024 NSDUH estimates are comparable with 2022-2023 estimates but not with 2020 or prior years. CDC's Alcohol-Related Disease Impact (ARDI) estimates from February 2024 onward should not be compared with earlier versions.

**Updated:** August 2025

## Prevalence of Lifetime Drinking

*People Ages 12 and Older*

According to the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 228.4 million people ages 12 and older (79.2% in this age group) reported that they drank alcohol at some point in their lifetime.1,2 This includes:

* 113.7 million males ages 12 and older (80.6% in this age group)1,2
* 114.7 million females ages 12 and older (77.9% in this age group)1,2
* 934,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 and older (68.5% in this age group)1,2
* 11.1 million Asian people ages 12 and older (59.7% in this age group)1,2
* 25.1 million Black or African American people ages 12 and older (71.1% in this age group)1,2
* 145.7 million White people ages 12 and older (85.4% in this age group)1,2
* 5.1 million people of two or more races ages 12 and older (79.2% in this age group)1,2
* 39.6 million Hispanic or Latino people ages 12 and older (72.5% in this age group)1,2
* Estimates for Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander people ages 12 and older were not presented because they were based on a relatively small number of respondents or had a large margin of error.1,2

*Youth Ages 12 to 17*

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 5.5 million youth ages 12 to 17 (21.3% in this age group) reported that they drank alcohol at some point in their lifetime.1,2 This includes:

* 2.6 million boys ages 12 to 17 (19.5% in this age group)1,2
* 3.0 million girls ages 12 to 17 (23.3% in this age group)1,2
* 46,000 American Indian or Alaska Native people ages 12 to 17 (22.1% in this age group)1,2
* 140,000 Asian youth ages 12 to 17 (9.2% in this age group)1,2
* 590,000 Black or African American youth ages 12 to 17 (16.5% in this age group)1,2
* 2.9 million White youth ages 12 to 17 (22.8% in this age group)1,2
* 238,000 youth of two or more races ages 12 to 17 (22.8% in this age group)1,2
* 1.6 million Hispanic or Latino youth ages 12 to 17 (23.5% in this age group)1,2
* Estimates for Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander youth ages 12 to 17 were not presented because they were based on a relatively small number of respondents or had a large margin of error.1,2

*Adults Ages 18 and Older*

## Emerging Trend—High-Intensity Drinking

High-intensity drinking is defined as consuming alcohol at levels that are two or more times the sex-specific binge drinking thresholds ([see glossary](/alcohols-effects-health/alcohol-topics-z/alcohol-facts-and-statistics/glossary "Glossary") for additional details about the definition of high-intensity drinking). Compared with people who did not binge drink, people who drank alcohol at twice the sex-specific binge drinking thresholds were 70 times more likely to have an alcohol-related emergency department visit, and those who consumed alcohol at three times the sex-specific binge thresholds were 93 times more likely to have an alcohol-related emergency department visit.11

According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), many (but not all) NSDUH estimates from 2024 are comparable with estimates from 2022, 2023, and updated 2021 estimates. However, 2021–2024 estimates are not comparable with 2020 or prior years' estimates. Please see the [2024 NSDUH Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/data-we-collect/nsduh-national-survey-drug-use-and-health/national-releases/2024) and section 2.3.4 of the [2024 Methodological Summary and Definitions report](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/report/2024-methodological-summary-and-definitions) for more details.

args.key_excerpts: According to the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 228.4 million people ages 12 and older (79.2% in this age group) reported that they drank alcohol at some point in their lifetime., In 2024, 85% of people ages 21 and older reported that they drank alcohol at some point in their lifetime., In 2024, 21.7% of people ages 18 and older reported that they engaged in binge drinking in the past month., Compared with people who did not binge drink, people who drank alcohol at twice the sex-specific binge drinking thresholds were 70 times more likely to have an alcohol-related emergency department visit, and those who consumed alcohol at three times the sex-specific binge thresholds were 93 times more likely to have an alcohol-related emergency department visit.
args.summary:
This webpage from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), part of the U.S. National Institutes of Health, presents comprehensive data on alcohol use in the United States based on the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH). The data is broken down by age groups (youth ages 12-17, adults ages 18+, and all people ages 12+) and demographic characteristics including sex, race, and ethnicity. The page covers five key prevalence measures:

**Lifetime Drinking (ages 12+):** 228.4 million people (79.2%) reported ever drinking alcohol. Among adults 18+, 85.0% reported lifetime drinking. Among youth 12-17, 21.3% reported lifetime drinking.

**Past-Year Drinking (ages 12+):** 178.7 million people (62.0%) reported drinking in the past year. Among adults 18+, 66.5% reported past-year drinking. Among youth 12-17, 16.4% reported past-year drinking.

**Past-Month Drinking (ages 12+):** 134.3 million people (46.6%) reported drinking in the past month. Among adults 18+, 50.6% reported past-month drinking. Among youth 12-17, 6.6% reported past-month drinking.

**Past-Month Binge Drinking (ages 12+):** 57.9 million people (20.1%) reported binge drinking in the past month. Among adults 18+, 21.7% reported binge drinking. Among youth 12-17, 3.5% reported binge drinking.

**Past-Month Heavy Alcohol Use (ages 12+):** 14.5 million people (5.0%) reported heavy alcohol use in the past month. Among adults 18+, 5.5% reported heavy alcohol use. Among youth 12-17, 0.4% reported heavy alcohol use.

The data reveals notable demographic patterns: White individuals had the highest prevalence across most drinking categories, while Asian individuals consistently had the lowest rates. Males generally reported higher rates of drinking than females across all categories. The page also highlights an emerging trend on high-intensity drinking, noting that people who drank at twice the binge threshold were 70 times more likely to have an alcohol-related emergency department visit, and those at three times the threshold were 93 times more likely. The page notes that 2024 NSDUH estimates are comparable with 2022, 2023, and updated 2021 estimates, but not with 2020 or prior years.

[Traci L. Toomey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Toomey%20T%22[Author])

Traci L. Toomey, Ph.D., is a research associate with, Carolyn Rosenfeld, M.P.H., is a recent graduate of, and Alexander C. Wagenaar, Ph.D., is a professor in the Division of Epidemiology, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521)Abstract

Minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) laws provide an example of how scientific research can support effective public policies. Between 1970 and 1975, 29 States lowered their MLDAs; subsequently, scientists found that traffic crashes increased significantly among teenagers. Alcohol use among youth is related to many problems, including traffic crashes, drownings, vandalism, assaults, homicides, suicides, teenage pregnancies, and sexually transmitted diseases. Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of a higher MLDA in preventing injuries and deaths among youth. Despite laws prohibiting the sale or provision of alcohol to people under age 21, minors can easily obtain alcohol from many sources. Increased MLDA enforcement levels and deterrents for adults who might sell or provide alcohol to minors can help prevent additional injuries and deaths among youth.

**Keywords:**minimum drinking age laws, evaluation, history of AOD public policy, public policy on AOD, adolescent, law enforcement, AOD availability, AOD sales, AODR (alcohol and other drug related) injury prevention, AODR mortality, traffic accident, drinking and driving

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521)History of the MLDA

Following the repeal of Prohibition, nearly all State laws restricting youth access to alcohol designated 21 as the minimum age for purchasing and consuming alcohol ([Mosher 1980](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b15-arhw-20-4-213)). Between 1970 and 1975, however, 29 States lowered the MLDA to age 18, 19, or 20. These changes occurred at the same time that minimum-age limits for other activities, such as voting, also were being lowered ([Wechsler and Sands 1980](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b38-arhw-20-4-213)). Scientists began studying the effects of the lowered MLDA, particularly focusing on traffic crashes, the leading cause of death among teenagers. Several studies in the 1970’s showed that traffic crashes increased significantly among teenagers after the MLDA was lowered ([Cucchiaro et al. 1974](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b3-arhw-20-4-213); [Douglass et al. 1974](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b4-arhw-20-4-213); [Wagenaar 1983](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b32-arhw-20-4-213), [1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b33-arhw-20-4-213); [Whitehead 1977](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b39-arhw-20-4-213); [Whitehead et al. 1975](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b40-arhw-20-4-213); [Williams et al. 1974](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b41-arhw-20-4-213)).

With evidence that lower legal drinking ages were associated with more traffic crashes among youth, citizen advocacy groups led a movement to restore the MLDA to 21 in all States ([Wolfson 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b42-arhw-20-4-213)). In response, 16 States increased their MLDA’s between September 1976 and January 1983 ([Wagenaar 1983](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b32-arhw-20-4-213)). Many States, however, resisted pressure from these groups and ignored Government incentives to raise their MLDA’s ([King 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b13-arhw-20-4-213)). The Federal Government became concerned about the safety both of youth in States that had lower MLDA’s and of youth who lived in neighboring States. Persons who were below the MLDA in their own State could drive across State borders to purchase alcohol in a State with a lower MLDA and then return home, increasing the likelihood of being involved in traffic crashes.

Because the 21st amendment to the U.S. Constitution guaranteed States’ rights to regulate alcohol, the Federal Government could not mandate a uniform MLDA of 21. Instead, in 1984 the Federal Government passed the Uniform Drinking Age Act, which provided for a decrease in Federal highway funding to States that did not establish an MLDA of 21 by 1987 ([King 1987](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b13-arhw-20-4-213)). Faced with a loss of funding, the remaining States returned their MLDA’s to age 21 by 1988.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521)Effectiveness of the MLDA

### Reductions in Drinking

Following the end of Prohibition, each State developed its own set of policies to regulate the distribution, sale, and consumption of alcohol. In addition to the MLDA, examples of other alcohol control policies include excise taxes, restrictions on hours and days of sales, and server training. Many of these other alcohol policies have only recently been evaluated (see [Toomey et al. 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b30-arhw-20-4-213) for a review of the research literature). Of all the alcohol control policies, MLDA policy has been the most studied. Since the 1970’s, at least 70 studies have explicitly examined the effects of either increases or decreases in the MLDA, with some studies using more robust research designs than others. MLDA policies may have been evaluated sooner and more often for a variety of reasons, including: (1) a growing concern about youth drinking and driving; (2) availability of archived, time-series data on traffic crashes; (3) the fact that many States first lowered, then raised, their MLDA’s; and (4) preliminary research showing the large effects of changes in MLDA’s. Thorough literature reviews by [Wagenaar (1983](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b32-arhw-20-4-213), [1993)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b33-arhw-20-4-213), the [United States General Accounting Office (1987)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b31-arhw-20-4-213), and [Moskowitz (1989)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b17-arhw-20-4-213) provide detailed summaries of many of these studies. MLDA laws have been evaluated mostly in terms of how changing the MLDA affects rates of alcohol use and traffic crashes among youth.

Methods used to study the effect of the MLDA on alcohol use have varied widely, contributing to differences in conclusions among studies. For example, some studies used convenience samples, such as students in introductory psychology classes, whereas other studies used sophisticated, random sampling designs to obtain nationally representative samples. [Wagenaar (1993)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b33-arhw-20-4-213) concluded that studies employing strong research and analytical designs typically observed increases in alcohol use among youth following a lowering of the MLDA. In contrast, when many States raised the MLDA, alcohol use among youth decreased.

Beer is the alcoholic beverage of choice for most youth. As a result, reduced rates of alcohol use among youth after the MLDA was increased were primarily evident in decreased rates of beer consumption ([Berger and Snortum 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b2-arhw-20-4-213)). Rates of wine and distilled spirits use among youth did not change dramatically following the rise in the MLDA ([Barsby and Marshall 1977](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b1-arhw-20-4-213); [Smart 1977](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b26-arhw-20-4-213)).

Opponents of the age-21 MLDA theorized that even if a higher MLDA reduced alcohol use among minors, drinking rates and alcohol-related problems would surge among those age 21 and older. In other words, opponents believed that a “rubber band” effect would occur: When youth turned 21, they would drink to “make up for lost time” and thus drink at higher rates than they would had they been allowed to drink alcohol at an earlier age. A study by [O’Malley and Wagenaar (1991)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b20-arhw-20-4-213), however, refutes this theory. Using a national probability sample, O’Malley and Wagenaar found that the lower rates of alcohol use due to a high legal drinking age continued even after youth turned 21.

Although the MLDA’s effect on youth alcohol consumption is important, a key consideration is whether the MLDA ultimately affects the rates of alcohol-related problems. Alcohol use among youth is related to numerous problems, including traffic crashes, drownings, vandalism, assaults, homicides, suicides, teenage pregnancies, and sexually transmitted diseases. Alcohol use is reported in one-fifth to two-thirds of many of these problems ([Howland and Hingson 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b10-arhw-20-4-213); [Plant 1990](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b21-arhw-20-4-213); [Roizen 1982](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b24-arhw-20-4-213); [Smith and Kraus 1988](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b28-arhw-20-4-213); [Strunin and Hingson 1992](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b29-arhw-20-4-213)). As drinking rates increase or decrease, rates of alcohol-related problems may change in response.

### Decreases in Traffic Crashes

Using various research methods, at least 50 studies have evaluated the effect of changes in the MLDA on traffic crashes ([Wagenaar 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b33-arhw-20-4-213)). Some studies assessed policy changes in only one State, whereas others analyzed the MLDA’s effect across multiple States. These studies evaluated the effect of MLDA changes on a variety of outcomes, including total traffic crash fatalities for youth; drinking-driving convictions; crashes resulting in injuries; and single-vehicle nighttime crash fatalities (the crashes most likely to involve alcohol).

Most studies on the effect of lowering the MLDA found an increase in traffic crashes and traffic deaths among youth ([Wagenaar 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b33-arhw-20-4-213)). Of the 29 studies completed since the early 1980’s that evaluated increases in the MLDA, 20 showed significant decreases in traffic crashes and crash fatalities. Only three clearly found no change in traffic crashes involving youth. The remaining six studies had equivocal results. Based on results from research studies such as these, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimated that in 1987 alone, 1,071 traffic crash fatalities were prevented because of the MLDA of 21 ([NHTSA 1989](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b18-arhw-20-4-213)).

Since 1984 researchers have been investigating whether changes in the MLDA also affect other alcohol-related problems. Of the four studies conducted to date that focused on other social and health consequences of alcohol use, three found an inverse relationship between the MLDA and alcohol-related problems: A higher legal drinking age was correlated with a lower number of alcohol problems among youth. The [New York State Division of Alcoholism and Alcohol Abuse (1984)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b19-arhw-20-4-213) found a 16-percent decrease in rates of vandalism in four States that raised the MLDA. In a study of an increase of the MLDA in Massachusetts, [Hingson and colleagues (1985)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b9-arhw-20-4-213) did not find significant changes in the rates of non-motor-vehicle trauma, suicide, or homicide. [Smith (1986)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b27-arhw-20-4-213), however, found an increase in non-traffic-related hospital admissions following decreases in the MLDA in two Australian states. [Jones and colleagues (1992)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b11-arhw-20-4-213) found lower rates of death caused by suicides, motor vehicle crashes, pedestrian accidents, and other injuries in States with higher MLDA’s. More research is needed to characterize the full effect of the MLDA on rates of alcohol-related injuries and on problems other than motor vehicle crashes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521)The Role of Enforcement

Research indicates that a higher MLDA results in fewer alcohol-related problems among youth and that the MLDA of 21 saves the lives of well over 1,000 youth each year ([NHTSA 1989](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b18-arhw-20-4-213); [Jones et al. 1992](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b11-arhw-20-4-213)). What is compelling is that the effect of the higher MLDA is occurring with little or no enforcement. A common argument among opponents of a higher MLDA is that because many minors still drink and purchase alcohol, an MLDA of 21 does not work. The evidence shows, however, that although many youth still consume alcohol, they drink less and experience fewer alcohol-related injuries and deaths than they did under lower MLDA’s ([Wagenaar 1993](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b33-arhw-20-4-213)). A more appropriate discussion, therefore, is not whether the MLDA should again be lowered but whether the current MLDA can be made even more effective.

Despite laws prohibiting the sale or provision of alcohol to people under age 21, minors throughout the United States can easily obtain alcohol from many sources. Buyers who appear to be younger than 21 can successfully purchase alcohol from licensed establishments without showing age identification in 50 percent or more of their attempts ([Forster et al. 1994](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b5-arhw-20-4-213), [1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b6-arhw-20-4-213); [Preusser and Williams 1992](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b22-arhw-20-4-213)). In addition, although many youth purchase alcohol themselves, most youth indicate that they generally obtain alcohol through social contacts over age 21 ([Wagenaar et al. 1996 _b_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b37-arhw-20-4-213); [Jones-Webb et al. in press](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b12-arhw-20-4-213)). These social contacts—who include friends, siblings, parents, coworkers, and strangers approached outside of alcohol establishments—purchase alcohol and then either provide or sell it to minors.

Commercial establishments licensed to sell alcohol, as well as social sources, face potential criminal penalties, fines, license suspensions, and lawsuits for selling or providing alcohol to minors. So why do they still supply alcohol to youth? One reason is that policies are not actively enforced. For policies to deter specific behaviors effectively, people must believe that they have some chance of being caught and that they will face swift consequences for noncompliance ([Gibbs 1975](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b7-arhw-20-4-213); [Ross 1992](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b25-arhw-20-4-213)). [Wolfson and colleagues (1996 _b_)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b46-arhw-20-4-213) found that only 38 percent of the alcohol merchants they surveyed thought it was likely that they would be cited for selling alcohol to a minor. Further research is needed to determine whether social sources are aware of their legal liability for providing alcohol to youth and whether they perceive a high likelihood of facing penalties for doing so.

Laws prohibiting the sale and provision of alcohol to minors are not well enforced ([Wagenaar and Wolfson 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b35-arhw-20-4-213)), and systems for enforcing the legislation vary by State. Typically, however, enforcement systems use both State administrative agencies, usually called State Alcohol Beverage Control (ABC) agencies, and local law enforcement agencies, such as police departments and county sheriffs. Enforcement of MLDA laws has focused primarily on penalizing underage drinkers for illegal alcohol possession or consumption ([Wagenaar and Wolfson 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b35-arhw-20-4-213)), an unintended and unanticipated consequence of the MLDA ([Mosher 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b16-arhw-20-4-213); [Wolfson and Hourigan in press](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b43-arhw-20-4-213)). For every 1,000 minors arrested for alcohol possession, only 130 establishments that sell alcohol to them have actions taken against them, and only 88 adults who purchase alcohol for minors face criminal penalties. [Wagenaar and Wolfson (1994)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b34-arhw-20-4-213) estimate that only 5 of every 100,000 incidents of minors’ drinking result in a fine, license revocation, or license suspension of an alcohol establishment.

An in-depth review of enforcement actions in 295 counties in 4 States (Kentucky, Michigan, Montana, and Oregon) showed that in a 3-year period, 27 percent of the counties took no action against licensed establishments for selling alcohol to minors, and 41 percent of those counties made no arrests of adults who provided alcohol to minors ([Wagenaar and Wolfson 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b35-arhw-20-4-213)). The States were selected for their diversity of alcohol-control systems and availability of data. Although the majority of counties took at least one action against alcohol establishments and adults who provided alcohol to youth, many did not take actions frequently.

As noted earlier, only a tiny proportion of incidents of minors’ drinking results in fines or other penalties for establishments that sell alcohol. Some reasons that enforcement agencies do not cite or arrest illegal providers include (1) perceived acceptance of underage drinking by community members, (2) lack of community encouragement to increase enforcement of the MLDA, and (3) lack of resources ([Wolfson et al. 1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b44-arhw-20-4-213)).

Given the low level of enforcement activity, it is not surprising that many adults do not hesitate to sell or give alcohol to minors. To create a deterrent effect, we need to increase the likelihood of facing negative consequences for illegally selling or providing alcohol to youth. One approach is to encourage ABC and local law enforcement agencies to increase enforcement against illegal alcohol providers. [Preusser and colleagues (1994)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b23-arhw-20-4-213) found dramatic reductions in alcohol sales to minors (from 59 percent at baseline to 26 percent 1 year later) following an enforcement campaign involving three “sting operations” in which underage males attempted to purchase alcohol.

In addition to increasing enforcement of the MLDA, other procedures and policies can be implemented to improve the effectiveness of MLDA laws. To ensure that adults do not sell or provide alcohol to minors, both public and institutional policies can be developed that complement MLDA laws ([Wagenaar et al. 1996 _a_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b36-arhw-20-4-213)). Alcohol establishments, for example, can implement several policies and practices, including (1) requiring all alcohol servers to receive responsible service training on how to check age identification and refuse sales to teenagers, (2) establishing systems to monitor servers to prevent illegal sales to youth, and (3) posting warning signs ([Wolfson et al. 1996 _a_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b45-arhw-20-4-213),[_b_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b46-arhw-20-4-213)). [Wolfson and colleagues (1996 _a_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b45-arhw-20-4-213),[_b_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b46-arhw-20-4-213)) found that establishments adhering to these policies were less likely to sell alcohol to young women who appeared to be under age 21 and who did not present age identification.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521)The Ongoing MLDA Debate

Despite an abundance of research demonstrating the effectiveness of the age-21 MLDA at saving lives and reducing alcohol-related problems, several States are again considering lowering their legal age limits for drinking. Louisiana’s MLDA of 21 was recently challenged in court on the premise that it violates the State’s constitutional law regarding age discrimination. Louisiana’s State Supreme Court concluded, however, that “. . . statutes establishing the minimum drinking age at a level higher than the age of majority are not arbitrary because they substantially further the appropriate governmental purpose of improving highway safety, and thus are constitutional” ([Manuel v. State of Louisiana [La. 1996]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b14-arhw-20-4-213)). In other words, because the MLDA was based on empirical evidence that such laws saved lives, the court decided that the law was not arbitrary and thus did not violate Louisiana’s constitution. Despite the Louisiana decision, the MLDA of 21 also may be challenged in other States.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521)Conclusion

The same arguments used to lower the MLDA 20 years ago are being used today (see [sidebar](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#bx1-arhw-20-4-213), pp. 216–217). Despite ongoing debates about the MLDA, research demonstrates the effectiveness of a higher MLDA in preventing alcohol-related injuries and deaths among youth. As the MLDA’s were lowered, rates of injuries and deaths increased; when the MLDA’s were raised, injuries and deaths significantly decreased. The benefit of using environmental (i.e., external) approaches, such as the MLDA, is further supported by the fact that drinking rates were reduced even after youth turned age 21. In contrast, individual approaches (e.g., school-based programs) have generated only short-term reductions in underage drinking. This finding suggests that to create long-term changes in youth drinking and alcohol-related problems, strategies that change the environment should be used.

### The Public Debate Over the MLDA

The public debate over reducing the legal drinking age has remained essentially unchanged since the minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) was first lowered in the 1970’s. Following are some frequently asked questions concerning the MLDA, along with answers based on the research findings to date.

**Question:** If States are the only entities that have the right to establish a minimum drinking age, does Federal legislation concerning this policy area infringe on State powers?

**Answer:** The initial movement to raise the MLDA to 21 was largely fueled by citizen action groups in several States, which raised their drinking ages before the Federal Government passed any legislation on the matter. Moreover, the Federal Government encouraged States to increase their MLDA’s to 21 to reduce traffic crashes caused by people driving to States that had lower MLDA’s. The Federal Government did not mandate the change. Polls continue to show strong public support for the drinking age of 21 ([Wagenaar 1993 _a_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b50-arhw-20-4-213)).

**Question:** Many Europeans let their children drink from an early age, and European countries do not have the same alcohol-related problems that we do. Therefore, how can people claim that MLDA’s are a major factor in helping to prevent alcohol problems in the United States?

**Answer:** Research confirms that European countries do experience alcohol-related problems. For example, European countries have rates of alcohol-induced diseases, such as cirrhosis of the liver, similar to (or higher than) the United States ([Single 1984](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b49-arhw-20-4-213)). Drunk driving among youth may not be as great a problem in Europe; compared with youth in the United States, European youth obtain their drivers’ licenses at an older age, are less able to afford automobiles, and more often use public transportation. Youth in Europe thus may be at lower risk of traffic crashes simply because they drive less frequently than their U.S. counterparts. Other alcohol-related problems are significant enough in Europe that those countries are examining the U.S. experience regarding MLDA policy and are initiating a debate over the most appropriate age for legal access to alcohol ([Wagenaar 1993 _a_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b50-arhw-20-4-213)).

In reviewing another country’s success with a given policy, one cannot simply compare international rates of alcohol-related problems without assessing the role of factors that contribute to the problems. Many cultural, political, and social conditions, which differ from country to country, affect drinking rates. The most robust research, although conducted in the United States, has shown a strong inverse relationship between MLDA and alcohol consumption and its related problems: As MLDA increases, alcohol-related problems among youth decrease. As MLDA changes occur in Europe, researchers will be able to determine more accurately the effect of a higher MLDA on alcohol-related problems among European youth.

**Question:** If a person is old enough to serve in the military, how can he or she not be old enough to buy alcohol?

**Answer:** Different activities have different ages of initiation: A person can drive at age 16, vote in elections and serve in the military at age 18, and serve as President at age 35. These restrictions are based on the requirements of the specific activities (e.g., motor skills, capacity for judgment, and experience) and take into account the risks and benefits of participation at different ages ([Fell 1985](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b47-arhw-20-4-213)). For example, research shows that at a given blood alcohol concentration, youth are more likely to be impaired than adults. Underage drinking is strongly related to serious public health problems, including injuries and death resulting from motor vehicle crashes, homicide, assault, and recreational injury. Consequently, policymakers and researchers have come to believe that risk both to youth and to society in general can be reduced by restricting people below age 21 from drinking.

**Question:** How can researchers be sure that the drop in rates of alcohol-related crashes among 19-and 20-year-olds following the increase in the MLDA to 21 was related to MLDA policy?

**Answer:** When the age-21 restriction was initiated, alcohol-involved highway crashes declined among 18- to 20-year-olds. This decline occurred with limited enforcement of the MLDA laws. The decline is therefore not attributable to drinking-driving enforcement and tougher penalties but directly results from lower consumption levels ([O’Malley and Wagenaar 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b48-arhw-20-4-213)).

**Question:** If people cannot legally drink until they are 21, will they just drink more when they reach the MLDA?

**Answer:** Research indicates that the opposite is true ([Wagenaar 1993 _b_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b51-arhw-20-4-213)). In fact, early legal access to alcohol (i.e., at age 18) is associated with higher rates of drinking later in life. Research shows that when the MLDA is 21, people under age 21 drink less and continue to do so through their early twenties. Those who are inclined to drink do not “make up for lost time” after turning 21 ([O’Malley and Wagenaar 1991](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6876521#b48-arhw-20-4-213)).

args.summary:
This scientific article from Alcohol Health Research World (1996) examines the Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA) in the United States. It reviews the history, effectiveness, enforcement, and ongoing debate surrounding MLDA laws.

**History:** Following Prohibition repeal, nearly all states set 21 as the minimum drinking age. Between 1970-1975, 29 states lowered their MLDA to 18, 19, or 20, concurrent with other age-limit reductions (e.g., voting). Studies showed traffic crashes increased significantly among teenagers after MLDA was lowered. In response, citizen advocacy groups pushed to restore MLDA to 21. Sixteen states raised their MLDA between 1976-1983, but many resisted. In 1984, the Federal Uniform Drinking Age Act incentivized states to adopt MLDA 21 by threatening reductions in federal highway funding; all states complied by 1988.

**Effectiveness:** MLDA is the most studied alcohol control policy, with at least 70 studies since the 1970s. Studies using strong research designs found alcohol use among youth increased when MLDA was lowered and decreased when raised. Higher MLDA reduced beer consumption among youth. Research refuted the "rubber band" theory that youth would binge at 21 to compensate. At least 50 studies evaluated MLDA effects on traffic crashes: 20 of 29 studies on MLDA increases showed significant decreases in crashes/fatalities; only 3 found no change. NHTSA estimated that in 1987 alone, 1,071 traffic crash fatalities were prevented due to MLDA 21. Studies on other alcohol-related problems (vandalism, suicides, hospital admissions) found higher MLDA correlated with fewer problems.

**Enforcement:** Despite laws, minors easily obtain alcohol from commercial and social sources. Underage buyers can successfully purchase alcohol 50% or more of the time without ID. Most youth obtain alcohol through social contacts over 21. Enforcement is minimal: only 38% of alcohol merchants thought they'd likely be cited for selling to minors. For every 1,000 minors arrested for possession, only 130 establishments face actions and only 88 adults face penalties. One study across 295 counties in 4 states found 27% took no action against establishments selling to minors. Enforcement campaigns involving sting operations reduced sales from 59% to 26%.

**Ongoing Debate:** Despite evidence of effectiveness, some states considered lowering the MLDA again. Louisiana's Supreme Court upheld the MLDA of 21, ruling it constitutional because it substantially furthers highway safety. The article concludes that a higher MLDA prevents alcohol-related injuries and deaths, and increased enforcement could prevent even more.

This is a 1999 research article published in the Annual Proceedings of the Association for the Advancement of Automotive Medicine, authored by Voas, Tippetts, and Fell. Using data from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) from 1982 to 1997 across all 50 states and DC, the researchers conducted a pooled cross-sectional time-series analysis using weighted least squares regression. The dependent variable was the odds ratio of drinking to non-drinking drivers under age 21 in fatal crashes. Key covariates included per capita beer consumption, vehicle miles traveled, unemployment rates, and other alcohol safety laws (per se .10 and .08 BAC laws, administrative license revocation, safety belt laws).

- The MLDA law was associated with an 18.9% reduction in the proportion of underage drinking drivers in fatal crashes.
- The zero tolerance law was associated with a 24.4% reduction.
- Per se .10 laws reduced underage drinking drivers by 17.8%, administrative license revocation by 19.0%, and safety belt laws by 20.6%.
- The .08 per se law showed a non-significant 6.4% reduction for underage drivers.
- Beer consumption was positively correlated with impaired underage drivers; safety belt laws were negatively correlated.

The study notes that alcohol-related traffic deaths for youth under 21 fell from 22 per 100,000 in 1982 to 10 per 100,000 in 1996. NHTSA estimated that through 1996, 16,513 lives were saved by MLDA laws. The authors acknowledge limitations, including potential confounding from changing public attitudes toward drinking and driving and the inability to fully separate the effects of individual laws from broader normative shifts.

A methodology update (first implemented for 2003 data) allocates fatalities from crashes with drivers of unknown age proportionally, rather than ignoring them. For 2003: using the old method yielded 885 lives saved; using the updated method yielded 906 lives saved. URL: https://www.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/alcohol-and-adolescent-brain

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) webpage provides research-based information on how alcohol affects the adolescent brain. Key points include:

**Adolescent Brain Development:** The brain undergoes complex developmental changes continuing into a person's mid-20s, making the adolescent brain particularly vulnerable to alcohol exposure.

**Patterns of Drinking:** Adolescents tend to drink less often than adults but drink more when they do drink. Binge drinking is defined as reaching BAC of 0.08%—for adolescents, fewer drinks are needed than adults to reach this level (3 drinks for females, 3-5 for males depending on age and size).

**Risk-Taking and Brain Plasticity:** Adolescents are motivated to explore and take risks, and while this plasticity provides learning opportunities, it also increases vulnerability to alcohol's negative effects. Early initiation of alcohol use is linked to unsafe behaviors including drinking and driving, unsafe sexual behavior, and other substance use.

**Immediate Effects:** Alcohol impairs decision-making and impulse control, disrupts the amygdala (fear-sensing), and can cause blackouts by blocking memory consolidation in the hippocampus. One in five older adolescents who ever drank reported an alcohol-induced blackout in the previous six months.

**Longer-Term Effects:** Adolescent alcohol use can increase likelihood of developing alcohol use disorder and is associated with anxiety and depression. Research shows reductions in the size of the frontal lobe, hippocampus, amygdala, and corpus callosum in heavy-drinking adolescents. However, the brain's plasticity during adolescence also lends itself to recovery from some alcohol-induced changes.

**Childhood Trauma Link:** Youth who experienced childhood trauma may have disrupted brain growth patterns that make them more likely to engage in binge drinking.

**Prevention:** Parents and teachers play a major role. Research shows children whose parents allow them to drink are more likely to transition quickly to unhealthy drinking patterns. Regular conversations and positive role modeling can shape healthy attitudes about alcohol.
</summary>

# NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts: Young Drivers (2020 Data)

## Overview
This fact sheet from NHTSA's National Center for Statistics and Analysis (June 2022, DOT HS 813 313) examines motor vehicle crash data for young drivers (ages 15-20) in 2020, based on FARS (fatal crash data) and CRSS (non-fatal crash data).

## Key Findings

- **Fatalities**: 1,885 young drivers died in traffic crashes in 2020, a 17% increase from 1,616 in 2019. Total fatalities in crashes involving young drivers reached 5,037 in 2020 — the highest in the 10-year period (2011-2020).
- **Injuries**: An estimated 189,950 young drivers were injured in 2020, a 7% decrease from 2019.
- **Licensed drivers**: Young drivers accounted for 11.6 million (5.1%) of all 228.2 million licensed drivers in 2020, a 4.7% decrease from 2019.
- **Crash involvement**: Young drivers were 8.5% of drivers in fatal crashes but only 5.1% of licensed drivers. Involvement in fatal crashes increased 14% (from 3,999 in 2019 to 4,561 in 2020), while police-reported crashes decreased 20%.
- **Gender disparity**: Male young driver fatal crash involvement rate: 56.59 per 100,000 licensed drivers vs. 21.54 for females — more than double.
- **Restraint use**: 52% of young drivers killed with known restraint use were unrestrained.
- **Alcohol**: 29% of young drivers killed (15-20) had BAC of .01+ g/dL; 82% of those with alcohol had BAC of .08+ g/dL. Despite being under the legal drinking age, alcohol involvement increases with age within this group.
- **Speeding**: Young male and female drivers had the highest speeding rates in fatal crashes compared to most other age groups.
- **Motorcycles**: 219 young motorcycle riders (15-20) killed in 2020; 27% of those killed were not wearing helmets (vs. 39% of all riders).
- **Driving records**: 15.5% of young drivers in fatal crashes with invalid licenses had prior license suspensions/revocations.
- **State data**: Texas had the highest number of young driver fatalities (207) and total fatalities in young-driver crashes (558). Percentages of traffic fatalities in young-driver crashes ranged from 8.7% (NH) to 17.8% (ID), with a national average of 13.0%.

## Long-term Trends (2011-2020)
In crashes involving young drivers: young driver fatalities decreased 5%, passenger fatalities decreased 9%, occupants of other vehicles increased 32%, and nonoccupant fatalities increased 24%. Total fatalities in these crashes increased 5% over the decade.

## Safety Reminders for Young Drivers and Parents
The report includes guidance on seat belt use, avoiding alcohol, no speeding, no distractions, understanding GDL laws, and parental involvement in teen driving.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Minimum Drinking Age Of 21 Saves Lives, Study Finds | ScienceDaily ---
URL: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2008/07/080701083542.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A study published in the July 2008 issue of Accident Analysis and Prevention, led by James C. Fell of the Pacific Institute for Research and Evaluation (PIRE), found that minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) laws of 21 save lives by reducing alcohol-related traffic fatalities among youth. The study analyzed FARS data from 1982-2004 and controlled for more variables than previous research, including vehicle safety improvements, better roadways, and tougher adult drunk driving laws. Key findings include: (1) laws making it illegal to possess or purchase alcohol for those under 21 led to an 11% drop in alcohol-related traffic deaths among youth; (2) states with strong laws against fake IDs reported 7% fewer alcohol-related fatalities among drivers under 21. The research was prompted by the 1984 federal legislation that threatened loss of highway funds unless states raised the drinking age to 21, which all states had done by 1988. From 1988 to 1995, alcohol-related traffic fatalities for youth aged 15-20 declined from 4,187 to 2,212 (a 47% decrease). The study was funded by the Substance Abuse Policy Research Program (SAPRP) of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There has been evidence since the 1980s that an increase in the drinking age to 21 was having an impact on traffic deaths," Fell said. "But this is the first time we've been able to tease out the real effect, free of the variables that had been used to question the validity of the evidence.", "States that merely confiscate a fake ID, or just give a slap on the wrist to the user, are passing up a significant opportunity to save lives," said Fell. "We found a seven percent drop in youth alcohol-related fatalities in states that are willing to take strong actions, such as automatically suspending the driver's license of a young person caught with a fake ID.", "Some have argued that the declining numbers are due to a general decrease in drunk driving, or because of the lowering of the BAC limit, or better cars and better roads. But we controlled for all of these to the extent possible in this study."

--- SOURCE 7: [PDF] Frequently Asked Questions: Minimum Legal Drinking Age/Age 21 - ERIC ---
URL: https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED537670.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This FAQ-style webpage presents research-supported arguments in favor of maintaining the U.S. Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA) of 21. Key points include:

1. **European comparison**: Contrary to myth, European youth have higher rates of alcohol consumption, intoxication, and related problems than American youth. European countries have higher per capita alcohol consumption and cirrhosis death rates. Lower alcohol-related crash rates in Europe are attributed to higher driving ages, expensive cars, and better public transit, not responsible drinking.

2. **Historical "natural experiment"**: Between 1970-1975, 29 states lowered drinking ages, leading to marked increases in alcohol-related teen crashes. When age 21 was restored, crashes immediately declined. Similarly, New Zealand's 1999 lowering from 20 to 18 resulted in more alcohol-involved crashes, emergency department visits, drunk driving, and disorderly conduct.

3. **Effectiveness of age 21**: After MLDA 21 was implemented, alcohol-involved crashes declined immediately (starting the next month). A 2008 study found an 11% drop in alcohol-related traffic deaths among under-21s. NHTSA estimates MLDA 21 saved 21,887 lives through 2002 and continues to save ~1,000 lives annually.

4. **Education programs**: Alcohol education alone has been proven ineffective at reducing high-risk drinking when used in isolation.

5. **Public support**: 77% of Americans oppose lowering the drinking age to 18 (2007 Gallup poll), with support nearly identical to 1984 levels.

6. **Underage drinking persists**: While some youth still drink, studies show they consume less and suffer fewer injuries when the drinking age is 21. Delaying onset of drinking reduces later alcohol dependence risk.

7. **Brain development**: Adolescent brains undergo changes that make them more susceptible to long-term alcohol impairments, affecting decision-making, impulse control, and memory. Heavy drinking teens showed significantly smaller hippocampi (10%).

8. **Effective strategies**: Combining MLDA 21 with enforcement efforts and increased beer taxes shows most promise for reducing alcohol-related harm.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Grabbing the Forbidden Fruit: Restriction-Sensitive Choice ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.11673

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper (arXiv:2509.11673v2, dated May 15, 2026) by Niels Boissonnet and Alexis Ghersengorin proposes a formal economic model called "restriction-sensitive choice" (RSC) to capture the "forbidden fruit effect" (FFE)—the phenomenon where restricting access to opportunities increases their desirability. The model axiomatizes how individuals react to restrictions, compatible with reactance theory and commodity theory from psychology.

**Key contributions:**
- The RSC model characterizes choice behaviors where removing an option causes a choice reversal (violating standard economic axioms like the Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives).
- The decision-maker categorizes options into "types" and uses a two-step procedure: first evaluating options within types using a welfare preference (≿1), then using a "reaction preference" (≿2) across types.
- **Theorem 1**: A choice function satisfies three axioms (Expansion, No-Reaction Comparability, and Independent Reaction) if and only if it is an RSC.
- **Theorem 2**: Adding the Single-Peaked Reaction axiom yields "single-peaked RSC," where the propensity to react increases with the severity of restriction up to a point, then declines.
- The model is identifiable from choice data: comparability classes, thresholds, and the peak of reaction preferences can be recovered from observed choice reversals (Propositions 1–3).
- The welfare criterion uses ≿1 (the welfare preference) as the normative benchmark, distinguishing genuine welfare from restriction-driven reactions.
- Applications include explaining the "backfire effect" in beliefs (e.g., reactions to media restrictions) and backlash against integration policies targeting minorities.

**Comparison to existing literature:** RSC is a specific case of transitive shortlist methods but satisfies additional axioms (NRC, SPR) that other models in the literature do not satisfy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"According to the Italian adage 'I frutti proibiti sono i piu dolci' (forbidden fruits are the sweetest), individuals have a natural tendency to place a higher value on things that are prohibited or unavailable.", "We axiomatize a choice model named restriction-sensitive choice (RSC), which rationalizes the forbidden fruit effect and is compatible with the prominent psychological explanations: reactance theory and commodity theory.", "The FFE poses an intriguing challenge to choice theory as it contradicts the standard model of preference (or utility) maximization, which entails that the 'Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives' (IIA)...", "According to RSC, the decision-maker (DM) categorizes the options into different types... When deprived of access to sufficiently good options from one type, the DM may be willing to react by reversing their choice in favor of a less good option of that type.", "We apply our model to shed light on two phenomena: the backfire effect of beliefs and the backlash of integration policies targeted towards minorities."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Underage Drinking and the Drinking Age - Hoover Institution ---
URL: https://www.hoover.org/research/underage-drinking-and-drinking-age

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Policy Review article from the Hoover Institution (June/July 2009) by Carla T. Main, critically examining the Amethyst Initiative—a movement led by 135 college presidents and chancellors calling for the reexamination of the 21 minimum drinking age. The article argues against lowering the drinking age, presenting extensive evidence to counter the Initiative's claims.

**Key arguments and evidence presented:**

**The Amethyst Initiative's position:** The Initiative, circulated by former Middlebury College president John McCardell, argues that the 21 laws are "not working," drive underage drinking underground, promote binge drinking through the "forbidden fruit" effect, and prevent open discussion about responsible alcohol use. It advocates for lowering the drinking age to 18 with licensing requirements.

**Historical context:** Between 1970-1976, 29 states lowered the drinking age, resulting in skyrocketing highway deaths among teens. By 1984, most had raised it back. The 1984 Uniform Drinking Age Act required states to set the minimum age at 21 to receive federal highway funds.

**Binge drinking statistics:** Among college students, 80% report drinking, with 40% binge drinking monthly—more than double the rate of non-college peers. Consequences include approximately 1,100 alcohol-related traffic deaths annually, 300 nontraffic alcohol-related deaths, 100,000 sexual assault incidents, 700,000 assaults, and 474,000 cases of unprotected sex due to drinking. The social cost of underage drinking is estimated at $53 billion.

**Countering the Initiative's claims:**
- U.S. military data shows soldiers drink *more* when alcohol is legal (25% heavy users outside U.S. vs. 15% in U.S.), contradicting the "forbidden fruit" theory.
- European countries with lower drinking ages experience worse binge drinking problems, particularly in the UK, Ireland, and Nordic countries.
- When New Zealand lowered its drinking age to 18, it experienced a "sharp increase in binge drinking among teenagers and young adults."
- Social-norms marketing programs on campuses have been shown to *increase* drinking, not decrease it.
- Education alone has not been proven effective in reducing binge drinking.

**Prohibition comparison:** The author argues the 21 laws are not analogous to Prohibition—they do not ban an industry, create bootleg markets, or foster organized crime. Underage drinkers obtain alcohol easily through fake IDs, older friends, and low-priced beer near campuses (as cheap as 25 cents per pitcher).

**Conclusion:** The article argues that the 21 laws should be enforced more rigorously rather than abandoned, noting that underage drinkers account for 19.4% of alcohol revenues ($22.5 billion). The author calls for political will to enforce existing laws, increase alcohol prices, and regulate liquor-selling establishments near campuses.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Amethyst Initiative's statement has been signed by 135 college presidents and chancellors at schools from Duke to Bennington. The statement says '21 is not working' and asks 'How many times must we relearn the lessons of Prohibition?'", "Among college students, 80 percent reported drinking and of those, 40 percent binge drink once a month — that is more than twice the rate of their peers in the general population.", "The U.S. Department of Defense...found high rates of binge drinking among young service members, especially men aged 18 to 25...The study found that one of the factors that made binge drinking less likely was being located in the United States." (Contradicting the forbidden fruit theory), "Underage drinkers account for 19.4 percent of alcohol revenues (about $22.5 billion). The absurdly low price of beer near college campuses — it is not unusual for a pitcher of beer to cost 25 cents — creates temptations that are very hard for young people in college to resist.", "Given the stakes, America should not throw in the towel on the 21 laws until we have actually enforced them as they were meant to be enforced — though it will require a clear dedication of political will."

--- SOURCE 4: The United States Limits Drinking by Youth Under Age 21: Does this Reduce Fatal Crash Involvements? ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3400235

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a 1999 research article published in the Annual Proceedings of the Association for the Advancement of Automotive Medicine, authored by Voas, Tippetts, and Fell. The study evaluates the effectiveness of US laws limiting youth drinking — specifically Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA) laws (age 21) and zero tolerance laws (0.02 BAC limit for drivers under 21) — in reducing alcohol-related fatal crash involvements among drivers under age 21.

Using data from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS) from 1982 to 1997 across all 50 states and DC, the researchers conducted a pooled cross-sectional time-series analysis using weighted least squares regression. The dependent variable was the odds ratio of drinking to non-drinking drivers under age 21 in fatal crashes. Key covariates included per capita beer consumption, vehicle miles traveled, unemployment rates, and other alcohol safety laws (per se .10 and .08 BAC laws, administrative license revocation, safety belt laws).

Key findings:
- The MLDA law was associated with an 18.9% reduction in the proportion of underage drinking drivers in fatal crashes.
- The zero tolerance law was associated with a 24.4% reduction.
- Per se .10 laws reduced underage drinking drivers by 17.8%, administrative license revocation by 19.0%, and safety belt laws by 20.6%.
- The .08 per se law showed a non-significant 6.4% reduction for underage drivers.
- Beer consumption was positively correlated with impaired underage drivers; safety belt laws were negatively correlated.

The study notes that alcohol-related traffic deaths for youth under 21 fell from 22 per 100,000 in 1982 to 10 per 100,000 in 1996. NHTSA estimated that through 1996, 16,513 lives were saved by MLDA laws. The authors acknowledge limitations, including potential confounding from changing public attitudes toward drinking and driving and the inability to fully separate the effects of individual laws from broader normative shifts.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Alcohol and the Adolescent Brain | National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) ---
URL: https://www.niaaa.nih.gov/publications/alcohol-and-adolescent-brain

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) webpage provides research-based information on how alcohol affects the adolescent brain. Key points include:

**Adolescent Brain Development:** The brain undergoes complex developmental changes continuing into a person's mid-20s, making the adolescent brain particularly vulnerable to alcohol exposure.

**Patterns of Drinking:** Adolescents tend to drink less often than adults but drink more when they do drink. Binge drinking is defined as reaching BAC of 0.08%—for adolescents, fewer drinks are needed than adults to reach this level (3 drinks for females, 3-5 for males depending on age and size).

**Risk-Taking and Brain Plasticity:** Adolescents are motivated to explore and take risks, and while this plasticity provides learning opportunities, it also increases vulnerability to alcohol's negative effects. Early initiation of alcohol use is linked to unsafe behaviors including drinking and driving, unsafe sexual behavior, and other substance use.

**Immediate Effects:** Alcohol impairs decision-making and impulse control, disrupts the amygdala (fear-sensing), and can cause blackouts by blocking memory consolidation in the hippocampus. One in five older adolescents who ever drank reported an alcohol-induced blackout in the previous six months.

**Longer-Term Effects:** Adolescent alcohol use can increase likelihood of developing alcohol use disorder and is associated with anxiety and depression. Research shows reductions in the size of the frontal lobe, hippocampus, amygdala, and corpus callosum in heavy-drinking adolescents. However, the brain's plasticity during adolescence also lends itself to recovery from some alcohol-induced changes.

**Childhood Trauma Link:** Youth who experienced childhood trauma may have disrupted brain growth patterns that make them more likely to engage in binge drinking.

**Prevention:** Parents and teachers play a major role. Research shows children whose parents allow them to drink are more likely to transition quickly to unhealthy drinking patterns. Regular conversations and positive role modeling can shape healthy attitudes about alcohol.
</summary>

**Dangers of Underage Drinking:** Alcohol is a significant factor in deaths of people under 21 each year, including from motor vehicle crashes, homicides, alcohol overdoses, and suicides. It causes injuries, impairs judgment, increases risk of physical and sexual assault, can lead to trouble in school or with the law, increases risk of alcohol use disorder (AUD) later in life, and interferes with brain development (which continues into the 20s).

**Warning Signs:** Mood changes, academic problems, rebelliousness, changing friend groups, low energy, finding alcohol, smelling alcohol on breath, coordination problems, slurred speech, among others.

**Treatment:** Screening by healthcare providers is recommended for all youth. Professional treatment includes individual/group counseling, prescription medications (for 18+), and family therapy.

<summary>

Key findings include:
- Alcohol use prevalence rises dramatically from 9.3% at age 12 to 89.8% at age 21. Heavy episodic drinking peaks at 50.5% by age 22.
- College students face significant consequences: 1,825 annual deaths from alcohol-related injuries, 599,000 injuries, 646,000 assaults, and 97,000 sexual assaults. Among surveyed students, 31% met criteria for alcohol abuse and 6% for alcohol dependence.

This fact sheet from NHTSA's National Center for Statistics and Analysis (June 2022, DOT HS 813 313) examines motor vehicle crash data for young drivers (ages 15-20) in 2020, based on FARS (fatal crash data) and CRSS (non-fatal crash data).

<summary>
A study published in the July 2008 issue of Accident Analysis and Prevention, led by James C. Fell of the Pacific Institute for Research and Evaluation (PIRE), found that minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) laws of 21 save lives by reducing alcohol-related traffic fatalities among youth. The study analyzed FARS data from 1982-2004 and controlled for more variables than previous research, including vehicle safety improvements, better roadways, and tougher adult drunk driving laws. Key findings include: (1) laws making it illegal to possess or purchase alcohol for those under 21 led to an 11% drop in alcohol-related traffic deaths among youth; (2) states with strong laws against fake IDs reported 7% fewer alcohol-related fatalities among drivers under 21. The research was prompted by the 1984 federal legislation that threatened loss of highway funds unless states raised the drinking age to 21, which all states had done by 1988. From 1988 to 1995, alcohol-related traffic fatalities for youth aged 15-20 declined from 4,187 to 2,212 (a 47% decrease). The study was funded by the Substance Abuse Policy Research Program (SAPRP) of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There has been evidence since the 1980s that an increase in the drinking age to 21 was having an impact on traffic deaths," Fell said. "But this is the first time we've been able to tease out the real effect, free of the variables that had been used to question the validity of the evidence.", "States that merely confiscate a fake ID, or just give a slap on the wrist to the user, are passing up a significant opportunity to save lives," said Fell. "We found a seven percent drop in youth alcohol-related fatalities in states that are willing to take strong actions, such as automatically suspending the driver's license of a young person caught with a fake ID.", "Some have argued that the declining numbers are due to a general decrease in drunk driving, or because of the lowering of the BAC limit, or better cars and better roads. URL: https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED537670.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This FAQ-style webpage presents research-supported arguments in favor of maintaining the U.S. Minimum Legal Drinking Age (MLDA) of 21. Key points include:

1. **European comparison**: Contrary to myth, European youth have higher rates of alcohol consumption, intoxication, and related problems than American youth. European countries have higher per capita alcohol consumption and cirrhosis death rates. Lower alcohol-related crash rates in Europe are attributed to higher driving ages, expensive cars, and better public transit, not responsible drinking.

2. **Historical "natural experiment"**: Between 1970-1975, 29 states lowered drinking ages, leading to marked increases in alcohol-related teen crashes. When age 21 was restored, crashes immediately declined. Similarly, New Zealand's 1999 lowering from 20 to 18 resulted in more alcohol-involved crashes, emergency department visits, drunk driving, and disorderly conduct.

3. **Effectiveness of age 21**: After MLDA 21 was implemented, alcohol-involved crashes declined immediately (starting the next month). A 2008 study found an 11% drop in alcohol-related traffic deaths among under-21s. NHTSA estimates MLDA 21 saved 21,887 lives through 2002 and continues to save ~1,000 lives annually.

4. **Education programs**: Alcohol education alone has been proven ineffective at reducing high-risk drinking when used in isolation.

5. **Public support**: 77% of Americans oppose lowering the drinking age to 18 (2007 Gallup poll), with support nearly identical to 1984 levels.

6. **Underage drinking persists**: While some youth still drink, studies show they consume less and suffer fewer injuries when the drinking age is 21. Delaying onset of drinking reduces later alcohol dependence risk.

7. **Brain development**: Adolescent brains undergo changes that make them more susceptible to long-term alcohol impairments, affecting decision-making, impulse control, and memory. Heavy drinking teens showed significantly smaller hippocampi (10%).

8. **Effective strategies**: Combining MLDA 21 with enforcement efforts and increased beer taxes shows most promise for reducing alcohol-related harm.
</summary>

This academic paper by Christopher Carpenter and Carlos Dobkin examines the public health impact of the U.S. minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) of 21, directly addressing claims made by the Amethyst Initiative (a group of college presidents calling for a reexamination of the drinking age). The paper uses two rigorous empirical approaches—a state-level panel fixed-effects model and a regression discontinuity design—to estimate the causal effects of the MLDA on alcohol consumption, mortality, nonfatal injury, and crime.

Key findings include:

- Arrest rates increase by 11% at age 21, concentrated in nuisance and violent crimes.
- Alcohol consumption (participation, heavy episodic drinking, and frequency) all increase significantly when the MLDA is lowered.

The authors conclude that the evidence clearly shows the age-21 drinking limit reduces alcohol consumption and its major harms. They provide a framework for weighing the costs and benefits, noting that the costs per drink (borne by the drinker and others) provide a lower bound for evaluating whether the policy is justified. The estimates imply that of the total reduction in teenager-involved fatalities due to MLDA equalization, for 18-year-olds between a quarter and a third and for 19-year-olds over 15 percent was due to this equalization. The results suggest that previous studies ignoring MLDA evasion have significantly understated the potential reduction in teenage drunk driving from completely restricting alcohol access, because local restrictions are partly evaded, often with fatal consequences.
