You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
* [Home](/)
* [Health](/health)
* [Neuroscience](/neuroscience)

# Germany Abolishes Supervised Drinking for Teens at 14 After Science Debunks Safety Myth

#### Federal cabinet cites brain research showing alcohol harms adolescents regardless of parental presence

By   [Morris Robinson](https://www.techtimes.com/reporters/morris-robinson)

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324218/20260812/germany-abolishes-supervised-drinking-teens-14-after-science-debunks-safety-myth.htm) [Share on Twitter](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Germany+Abolishes+Supervised+Drinking+for+Teens+at+14+After+Science+Debunks+Safety+Myth+https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324218/20260812/germany-abolishes-supervised-drinking-teens-14-after-science-debunks-safety-myth.htm) [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.techtimes.com%2Farticles%2F324218%2F20260812%2Fgermany-abolishes-supervised-drinking-teens-14-after-science-debunks-safety-myth.htm&title=Germany+Abolishes+Supervised+Drinking+for+Teens+at+14+After+Science+Debunks+Safety+Myth) [Share on Reddit](http://reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324218/20260812/germany-abolishes-supervised-drinking-teens-14-after-science-debunks-safety-myth.htm&title=Germany+Abolishes+Supervised+Drinking+for+Teens+at+14+After+Science+Debunks+Safety+Myth) [Share on Flipboard](https://flipboard.com) [Share on Pocket](https://getpocket.com/edit?url=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324218/20260812/germany-abolishes-supervised-drinking-teens-14-after-science-debunks-safety-myth.htm)

Sérgio Alves Santos/unsplash.com

Germany's federal cabinet approved legislation Wednesday that bans all alcohol consumption by teenagers under the age of 16 with no parental exception — using a body of neurological research to invalidate a 70-year cultural assumption that [supervised drinking at home](https://www.t-online.de/nachrichten/deutschland/innenpolitik/id_101385496/bundeskabinett-schafft-begleitetes-trinken-fuer-jugendliche-ab.html) was safer than prohibition. The bill now moves to the Bundestag for a final vote that is widely expected to pass, given the broad coalition that has aligned behind it.

### What Was the Supervised-Drinking Rule — and Why Did It Exist?

The provision being eliminated, known in German as *begleitetes Trinken* — literally "accompanied drinking" — was first codified in the *Jugendschutzgesetz*, Germany's [Youth Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protection_of_Young_Persons_Act_(Germany)), when the law came into force in 1952. Under its terms, 14- and 15-year-olds could legally purchase and consume beer, wine, and sparkling wine in public, provided a parent or legal guardian was present and consenting. The rule formalized what had been a longstanding German cultural assumption: that introducing teenagers to alcohol under adult supervision was a harm-reduction strategy — teaching responsible drinking while preventing illicit, unsupervised binge sessions.

For more than seven decades, this assumption went largely unchallenged in German law, even as European peers moved toward stricter age floors. France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, and the Netherlands all require a minimum age of 18 for all alcohol purchases. Germany's own standard for unsupervised beer and wine consumption remains 16 — above only Belgium, Denmark, and a handful of other countries in Western Europe — while the supervised-drinking provision for 14- and 15-year-olds had no close parallel among Germany's Western European neighbors.

The cabinet's draft bill is blunt about why the exception must go: the provision "weakens the protection of young people from the dangers of alcohol abuse and thus [contradicts the federal government's objectives](https://www.t-online.de/nachrichten/deutschland/innenpolitik/id_101385496/bundeskabinett-schafft-begleitetes-trinken-fuer-jugendliche-ab.html) of better addiction prevention," it states.

### Brain Science Made the Case Parental Supervision Couldn't

The political momentum behind ending *begleitetes Trinken* built over years, but it accelerated as neuroscience dismantled the premise the rule was built on.

The adolescent brain is not simply a smaller adult brain — it is an organ in active construction, with the prefrontal cortex (the region governing impulse control, decision-making, and executive function) continuing to develop into the mid-twenties. The hippocampus, responsible for learning and memory formation, is equally unfinished. Studies using structural MRI have found that adolescent heavy drinkers show measurably thinner prefrontal cortex volumes and reduced hippocampus size compared with non-drinking peers, with the [hippocampus and related limbic structures](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2022.1040049/full) among the most vulnerable brain regions. Alcohol does not merely impair these structures temporarily: it disrupts the ongoing neurogenesis and myelination processes that [permanently alter structural development](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3149806/).

What this means for the supervised-drinking debate is that the question was never whether a parent was in the room. Ethanol does not moderate its neurological effects in response to parental presence.

Research published in *European Psychiatry* in March 2026 found that children exposed to alcohol at a young age are significantly more likely to experience problematic alcohol use in late adolescence, even after controlling for sociocultural and other differences — and that early alcohol sipping was specifically predictive of later alcohol-related problems regardless of the context in which it occurred, according to the [prospective cohort study](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-psychiatry/article/parental-alcohol-supply-in-early-childhood-and-adolescent-drinking-evidence-from-a-prospective-cohort/E5BA0C7D150A717418FBEDC37856CCB3). A study published in *Addictive Behaviors* in 2025 reviewed nine annual waves of longitudinal data and found that "irrespective of the age of onset, parental permission to drink alcohol confers risk to adolescents for [later alcohol use and related harms](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0306460325000267)." The Institute of Alcohol Studies, reviewing University at Buffalo research, concluded that [allowing supervised teen drinking](https://www.ias.org.uk/2025/04/08/despite-what-many-parents-think-allowing-teenagers-to-try-alcohol-at-any-age-is-harmful/) actually increases the risk of later alcohol use and harmful drinking — and that the age at which parents allow it makes no difference.

Germany's own health data underlined the urgency. In 2024, around 7.9 million Germans aged 18 to 64 consumed alcohol at levels classified as risky — meaning they faced elevated risk of health or social problems, [according to DHS data](https://www.dhs.de/fileadmin/user_upload/pdf/pressemitteilungen/2026-04-16_PM_Jahrbuch_Sucht_2026.pdf). Alcohol is linked to roughly 44,000 deaths in Germany annually, according to the [German Centre for Addiction Issues (DHS)](https://www.dhs.de/fileadmin/user_upload/pdf/pressemitteilungen/2026-04-16_PM_Jahrbuch_Sucht_2026.pdf). The total social and economic cost — factoring in healthcare spending, lost productivity, early retirement, and alcohol-related deaths — was estimated at approximately €57 billion (approximately $65.7 billion USD) in 2024.

### How Germany Got Here: A Coalition Built Over Years

The cabinet vote did not emerge from a single political moment. The reform arrived after a sustained alignment of institutional forces.

Germany's state health ministers, led by an initiative from Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in June 2025, called for the exception's abolition, citing neuroscience showing that parental oversight does not reduce neurological risk from adolescent alcohol exposure. The *Bundesrat* — Germany's upper house, representing the country's sixteen states — [voted by a clear majority](https://www.bundesrat.de/drs.html?id=325-25%28B%29) in September 2025 in favor of scrapping the supervised-drinking rule.

A Forsa survey commissioned in 2025 by the KKH Kaufmännische Krankenkasse (a German commercial health insurer) found that nearly two-thirds of German adults — 65% — [support abolishing the *begleitetes Trinken* rule](https://www.kkh.de/presse/pressemeldungen/begleitetestrinken). A slim majority, 52%, said they would go further and raise the minimum age for beer and wine from 16 to 18 — a change not included in the current bill.

Family Minister Karin Prien of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) packaged the alcohol provision inside a broader reform of child and youth welfare — a 56-page bill restructuring responsibilities for children with disabilities in schools, foster family placements, and age verification for unaccompanied foreign minors. The alcohol provision sits somewhat apart from the structural reform's core, as Prien's ministry has acknowledged, but she chose to include it as a deliberate policy signal that Germany's addiction-prevention goals and its laws must align.

The bill's language is explicit: the supervised-drinking exception "stands in contradiction to the goals of the federal government concerning better addiction prevention."

### Does Prien's Portfolio Signal a Broader Age-Restriction Agenda?

The supervised-drinking ban is not Prien's only effort to regulate what teenagers are exposed to. In September 2025, she established an independent expert commission to set evidence-based policy on child digital safety — specifically regarding age limits on social media access, according to a [Library of Congress review](https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2026-07-28/germany-new-recommendations-published-on-digital-safety-for-children-and-young-people/). In July 2026, her ministry published the commission's interim recommendations; Prien publicly supported setting the minimum age for social media at 13 with effective age verification and graduated security measures up to 18, and called for a unified European solution. She has also overseen the €5 billion (approximately $5.76 billion USD) [Digital Pact 2.0](https://www.thelocal.de/20251222/government-confirms-plans-to-invest-five-billion-euros-in-digital-education) agreed in December 2025, which is investing in school digitalization across all 16 German states over five years.

Taken together, Prien is building a policy portfolio that applies the same logic to multiple domains: when evidence shows that unrestricted exposure to something — alcohol, social media — is harmful to developing brains and developmental outcomes, the state should set age-based limits backed by enforcement mechanisms. The alcohol and digital-safety efforts are not identical policy instruments, but they share an underlying framework: neuroscience and evidence-based harm prevention rather than cultural tradition or industry preference.

### Germany Is Still Not in Line With the European Majority

What Wednesday's vote does not do is close Germany's gap with the majority of EU member states.

The European mainstream requires 18 as the minimum age for all alcohol purchases and consumption. Germany, after this reform, will retain 16 as the floor for beer and wine, leaving it still among the more permissive jurisdictions in Western Europe — on par with Belgium and Denmark, and below the standard applied in France, Spain, Italy, Ireland, and the Netherlands.

Per-capita alcohol consumption in Germany was 115.1 liters (30.4 US gallons) per person in 2024, of which beer accounted for 88 liters (23.2 US gallons), according to the [DHS Yearbook of Addiction 2026](https://www.dhs.de/fileadmin/user_upload/pdf/pressemitteilungen/2026-04-16_PM_Jahrbuch_Sucht_2026.pdf). In terms of pure alcohol, Germany's per-capita consumption sits around 10.6 liters (2.8 US gallons) annually — above the EU average and down from a 2010 peak of 12.2 liters (3.2 US gallons). This places Germany in the upper tier of European consumers even as aggregate figures have trended downward.

That same neuroscience that the cabinet used to justify ending the 14-year exception applies, of course, to 16-year-olds as well — whose prefrontal cortex and hippocampal development are equally incomplete. The research does not draw a bright line at 14; it draws one at "adolescence," which researchers and physicians consistently define as extending into the mid-twenties. The Forsa survey's finding that 52% of Germans already favor raising the minimum to 18 suggests that the cabinet's vote today may not be Germany's final word on the question.

### What Happens Next

The bill passed to the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, for deliberation and a final vote. No specific date for that vote has been announced. Given that the Bundesrat has already endorsed the measure, all major political parties in the governing coalition are behind it, and polling shows clear public support, passage is widely expected before the end of 2026. An implementation timeline has not been set.

For German teenagers currently aged 14 and 15, the practical impact will be most visible at family occasions — confirmations, communions, weddings — where a supervised glass of Sekt or beer has been a generational tradition. If the Bundestag passes the bill as expected, those moments will no longer carry the state's sanction for the under-16s.

For German health authorities, the vote represents the first time legislation has formally acknowledged that the cultural premise of supervised drinking was not scientifically supportable — and that the legal framework must now reflect what neuroscience has known for years: the developing brain does not know whether a parent is watching.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can 14-year-olds still legally drink in Germany after this vote?

Not if the Bundestag passes the bill — which it is widely expected to do. The cabinet's approval removes the provision that previously allowed 14- and 15-year-olds to consume beer, wine, and sparkling wine in public when accompanied by a parent or legal guardian. Once the Bundestag votes and the law takes effect, the minimum age for all beer and wine consumption in Germany will be 16, with no parental exception. Spirits remain restricted to those 18 and older.

### Does science actually show that supervised drinking is harmful, or is this a political decision?

The scientific evidence is robust and consistent across multiple longitudinal studies. Research from the University at Buffalo, summarized by the Institute of Alcohol Studies, found that parental permission to drink increases the risk of later alcohol harm regardless of the age at which permission is granted. A March 2026 study in *European Psychiatry* found that early alcohol exposure — including supervised sipping — predicted alcohol-related problems in late adolescence even after controlling for sociocultural differences. The neuroscience is equally clear: the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus continue developing into the mid-twenties, and alcohol disrupts that development regardless of the presence of a supervising adult, as [neuroscience research on corticolimbic systems](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3149806/) has repeatedly shown.

### Will Germany eventually raise its drinking age to 18, in line with most EU countries?

That question is not settled. The current reform only abolishes the 14-year supervised-drinking exception; Germany's general minimum age for beer and wine remains 16. However, the same neurological evidence used to justify today's cabinet vote applies equally to 16-year-olds — whose brains are also still developing. A June 2025 Forsa survey found that 52% of Germans already favor raising the beer-and-wine minimum to 18, [according to the KKH Kaufmännische Krankenkasse](https://www.kkh.de/presse/pressemeldungen/begleitetestrinken), suggesting public opinion is ahead of current policy. Whether that majority translates into legislation will depend on political will that is not yet evident in the current coalition's agenda — but the scientific case for a further reform is already on the table.

### Does Germany's 70-year supervised-drinking rule have any equivalent in other EU countries?

No close parallel exists in Western Europe. While several EU countries, including Belgium and Denmark, share Germany's 16-year threshold for beer and wine, the specific provision allowing 14- and 15-year-olds to drink when supervised by a parent had no modern Western European counterpart. The majority of EU member states — including France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, Greece, and the Netherlands — set 18 as the minimum age for all alcohol, with no parental exception for younger teenagers, as confirmed by [comparative legal drinking age data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_drinking_age). Germany's former rule was a genuine outlier, not a reflection of a broader European norm.

args.summary:
Germany's federal cabinet approved legislation on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, that abolishes the country's 70-year-old "begleitetes Trinken" (accompanied drinking) provision, which allowed 14- and 15-year-olds to consume beer, wine, and sparkling wine in public when accompanied by a parent or legal guardian. The bill now moves to the Bundestag for a final vote, which is widely expected to pass before the end of 2026.

The reform was driven by a growing body of neurological research that debunked the cultural assumption that supervised drinking was safer than prohibition. Key scientific findings include:
- The adolescent brain's prefrontal cortex and hippocampus continue developing into the mid-twenties, and alcohol disrupts that development regardless of parental presence.
- A March 2026 study in *European Psychiatry* found early alcohol exposure predicted later alcohol-related problems even after controlling for sociocultural differences.
- A 2025 study in *Addictive Behaviors* found that "irrespective of the age of onset, parental permission to drink alcohol confers risk to adolescents for later alcohol use and related harms."
- University at Buffalo research concluded that allowing supervised teen drinking increases the risk of later harmful drinking.

The political momentum built over years, with Germany's state health ministers calling for abolition in June 2025, the Bundesrat voting in favor in September 2025, and a Forsa survey showing 65% public support. Family Minister Karin Prien (CDU) included the alcohol provision in a broader child and youth welfare reform bill.

After the reform, Germany's minimum age for beer and wine remains 16, still above the EU average and on par with Belgium and Denmark. The country's per-capita alcohol consumption is around 10.6 liters of pure alcohol annually, above the EU average. A Forsa survey found 52% of Germans already favor raising the minimum to 18, suggesting further reform may be possible.

# Germany to ban supervised drinking for teenagers

![Rachel Loxton](https://assets.thelocal.com/cdn-cgi/rs:fit:47/quality:75/plain/https://apiwp.thelocal.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/Rachel_Loxton.jpg@webp)

**[Rachel Loxton](/author/rachel-loxton-2)** - rachel.loxton@thelocal.com 

Published: 13 Aug, 2026 CET. Updated: Thu 13 Aug 2026 09:10 CET

* [2 comments](#article-comments)

 ![Germany to ban supervised drinking for teenagers](https://assets.thelocal.com/cdn-cgi/rs:fit:850/quality:75/plain/https://apiwp.thelocal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/AFP__20260423__A8R64CM__v1__MidRes__GermanyGastronomyTraditionDrinkAlcoholBeer.jpg@webp) 

A man raises glasses of beer in Munich, southern Germany on April 23, 2026, during a festive event to celebrate the National Day of German Beer. (Photo by Michaela STACHE / AFP)

 

A rule that allows 14 and 15-year-olds to drink alcohol in Germany when supervised by an adult is set to be scrapped.

A glass of sparkling wine for a grandchild at a birthday celebration, or a beer for a young guest at a wedding: in Germany, allowing teenagers to have an alcoholic drink in the company of their parents has long been part of social life.

But that tradition could soon come to an end.

The German Cabinet on Wednesday approved plans to scrap a rule that currently allows 14- and 15-year-olds to drink beer, wine or sparkling wine when accompanied by a responsible adult.

The proposal, put forward by Family Minister Karin Prien of the centre-right CDU, will soon be debated in the Bundestag.

The government had previously [considered raising the legal drinking age to 18.](https://www.thelocal.de/20250804/will-germany-raise-the-drinking-age-for-beer-and-wine) Instead, it aims to remove the special provision for younger teenagers, meaning the existing age limit of 16 for consuming beer, wine and sparkling wine will continue to apply – but without the exception.

"The exemption in the Youth Protection Act, which permits 14- and 15-year-olds to consume or purchase alcoholic drinks when accompanied by a person with parental responsibility, will be abolished," the draft states.

Prien argues that the current exemption weakens efforts to protect young people from the health and social consequences of alcohol, and goes against the government's goal of strengthening addiction prevention.

The proposal comes after growing concern among health officials about alcohol consumption among young people.

However, alcohol use rates were already declining. A 2024 study found that 6.9 percent of girls and 12.4 percent of boys aged between 12 and 17 drank alcohol at least once a week, less than half the number that did so in 2004.

**READ ALSO: ['Beer is cheap and everywhere' - How Germany's drinking culture surprises foreigners](https://www.thelocal.de/20250513/beer-is-cheap-and-everywhere-how-germanys-drinking-culture-surprises-foreigners)**

### Advertisement

**What are Germany's drinking laws?**

Germany's laws allowing younger people to drink may seem lax compared to many other countries.

Under Germany's current Youth Protection Act, 16- and 17-year-olds can buy and consume beer, wine, sparkling wine and drinks made from them in public.

Harder liquors – such as schnapps, vodka and whisky – remain restricted to those aged 18 and over.

At the moment, 14- and 15-year-olds can consume beer, wine or sparkling wine in public when accompanied by a parent or another adult with parental responsibility. If the proposed reform becomes law, this exemption would disappear.

In neighbouring France alcohol cannot legally be sold or offered to anyone under 18 in public, and there is no exception for teenagers.

Due to the risks of addiction, Germany's state health ministers spoke out in favour of a ban last year, and the Bundesrat launched a corresponding initiative.

The Federal Government’s Drug Commissioner, Hendrik Streeck, also spoke out in favour of the ban.

The Cabinet's decision is the first step. The proposal still needs to be approved by the Bundestag and Bundesrat before the change would be written into law.

# Will Germany end 'supervised drinking' for under-16s?

July 11, 2024

Germany's health minister is considering an end to "supervised drinking" in bars for minors between the ages of 14 and 16.

https://p.dw.com/p/4i9CF

Germany's approach to drinking at a young age is relaxed compared to most countriesImage: Annette Riedl/dpa/picture alliance

Advertisement

[Germany Health Minister Karl Lauterbach](/en/karl-lauterbach/t-60576642) is considering an end to the practice of "supervised drinking" for under-16s in bars when accompanied by a responsible adult.

[The country's laws](/en/germanys-drugs-czar-wants-tougher-rules-on-alcohol-tobacco-ads/a-64525272) are among the most relaxed in the world, with 14- to 16-year-olds allowed to drink beer, [wine, and wine-like beverages](/en/germanys-love-of-sparkling-wine-loses-its-fizz/a-67764433) under the supervision of a parent or guardian. The premise is that it is better to teach a responsible approach to alcohol rather than banning it.

## What are politicians saying?

Lauterbach, from the center-left [Social Democrats (SPD)](/en/social-democratic-party-spd/t-17437818), and other voices say the harm of such an approach outweighs any perceived benefit.

"From a health policy perspective, there can be no two opinions on this issue. So-called supervised drinking should be prohibited," Lauterbach told the German news network RND. "The presence of adults does not change the harmfulness of alcohol for children. That is why so-called supervised drinking should be prohibited."

[Bavarian](/en/bavaria/t-18968282) Health Minister Judith Gerlach, of the state's conservative Christian Social Union, has also called for an end to the current regulation.

"It makes no sense that young people aged 14 to 16 are allowed to consume alcohol in bars or restaurants if a person with parental responsibility accompanies them," said Gerlach.

Meanwhile, SPD [Berlin](/en/berlin/t-18967759) State Senator Ina Czyborra has also called for a change for health reasons, adding that the minimum age threshold of 18 in Germany's partial legalization of cannabis and the law on alcohol proved contradictory.

## Germany's risky alcohol consumption

## Does Germany have a drinking problem?

Germany had the fifth highest per capita alcohol consumption worldwide in a 2016 study, with the proportion of teenagers drinking alcohol in Germany among the highest in both Europe and the world.

Drinking in public places other than bars is generally legal and considered socially normal.

Christina Rummel, managing director of the German Center for Addiction Issues (DHS), has also called for a ban on supervised drinking.

"The earlier alcohol consumption begins, the greater the likelihood of addiction and the lower the likelihood of overcoming this addiction," Rummel warned.

Underage drinking in private is not regulated by a specific legal restriction in Germany. Here, the law is governed more by a parent's overall obligation to care for a child and protect them from physical and mental harm.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Aufse%C3%9F_Bier.JPG/330px-Aufse%C3%9F_Bier.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aufseß_Bier.JPG)

[Beer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_in_Germany "Beer in Germany") is an important part of [German culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_culture "German culture").

The [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") laws regulating [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_(drug) "Alcohol (drug)") use and sale are mostly focused on youth protection. In contrast to many other countries, legislation is relatively lenient and not designed to keep young people away from alcohol, but rather intended to teach them an appropriate approach to alcohol consumption, which is reflected by one of the lowest [drinking ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_drinking_age "Legal drinking age") in the world.

The tax rates for alcoholic beverages in Germany are below average compared to the rest of Europe, and there are very few regulations governing availability.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) [Drinking in public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drinking_in_public "Drinking in public") is generally legal and considered socially normal.[[2]](#cite_note-:1-2) Although the government has planned stricter regulations several times, the alcohol industry is politically influential and has prevented their implementation.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In 2006, approximately 1.7 million people in Germany were [dependent on alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_dependence "Alcohol dependence") and needed treatment, and 2.7 million [consumed alcohol in a harmful way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholism "Alcoholism").[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) In 2016, Germany had the [fifth highest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_alcohol_consumption_per_capita#Comprehensive_list_with_data_from_2016 "List of countries by alcohol consumption per capita") per capita alcohol consumption worldwide. The rate of teenagers drinking alcohol in Germany is one of the highest in both Europe[[7]](#cite_note-7) and the world.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Due to the low taxation on alcohol, low drinking age and lax regulations regarding availability, as well as a supposed social trivialization of the risks and harmfulness of alcohol in the country, Germany has been referred to as a paradise for drinkers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

## Drinking age

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Drinking age")]

See also: [Protection of Young Persons Act (Germany)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protection_of_Young_Persons_Act_(Germany) "Protection of Young Persons Act (Germany)")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Jugendschutzgesetz_%28Aushang%29.png/250px-Jugendschutzgesetz_%28Aushang%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jugendschutzgesetz_(Aushang).png)

**German Jugendschutzgesetz (Youth Protection Law):**  
The law has to be placed at every public event and establishments selling or serving alcoholic beverages.

In Germany, underage drinking in private is not regulated by a specific legal restriction. However, protection from physical and mental harm is part of parents' general obligation to care for a child.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Regarding alcohol purchase and alcohol consumption in public places (such as pubs and restaurants), Germany has three [drinking ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_drinking_age "Legal drinking age") regulated by *§ 9 Jugendschutzgesetz*[[12]](#cite_note-12) *(Protection of Young Persons Act)*:

> **§ 9 Alcoholic drinks**  
> (1) In licensed premises, at points of sale or elsewhere in public places
>
> 1. Beer, wine, wine-like beverages or sparkling wine or mixtures of beer, wine, wine-like beverages or sparkling wine and soft drinks, must not be sold to Children and Adolescents below the age of 16 years,
> 2. other alcoholic drinks or food items that contain other alcoholic drinks in more than insignificant quantities must not be sold to Children and Adolescents,
>
> nor must their consumption by said persons be tolerated.
>
> (2) Sub-Clause 1, No. 1 shall not apply to Adolescents accompanied by a Custodial Person.

— Protection of Young Persons Act, [§ 9 Alcoholic drinks](https://www.bmfsfj.de/blob/90278/7a45fcfc6a8f06a8fcca28df3274e947/juschg-englisch-2016-data.pdf)

**This results in three different drinking ages depending on the type of alcoholic beverage and circumstances:**

* **At 14** – Minors are allowed to consume and possess undistilled alcoholic beverages, such as [beer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer "Beer") and [wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine "Wine") in public places, bars or restaurants, as long as they are in the company and have the permission of a Custodial Person. *(§ 9 JuSchG (2) and § 1 JuSchG (1) 2)*. This regulation is colloquially known as "begleitetes Trinken" ("accompanied drinking") and is considered increasingly controversial in recent years, with two [SPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPD "SPD") politicians having called for its abolition.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)
* **At 16** – Minors are allowed to consume and possess undistilled alcoholic beverages, such as [beer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer "Beer") and [wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine "Wine") in public places, bars or restaurants without their parents or a Custodian. *(§ 9 JuSchG (1) 2)*.
* **At 18** – Having become adults, people are allowed access to [distilled spirits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distilled_beverage "Distilled beverage"), beverages containing distilled spirits, and food products containing non-negligible amounts of distilled spirits. *(§ 9 JuSchG (1) 1)*.

Those limits do not apply to married adolescents. *(§ 1 JuSchG (5))*.

### Debate on raising the drinking age

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Debate on raising the drinking age")]

Because of [moral panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_panic "Moral panic") involving excessive alcohol use among minors (a 16-year-old boy died after having consumed 45 shots of [tequila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tequila "Tequila") in a bar in early 2007),[[17]](#cite_note-17) some people demanded that the drinking age be raised. Most politicians, however, spoke against that notion, pointing out instead that such use was already forbidden according to current laws, which simply needed to be enforced.[[18]](#cite_note-18) In [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), alcohol consumption is traditional and very much publicly accepted compared to most other countries.[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6)

A study by the [RWI Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RWI_Essen "RWI Essen") found a correlation between reaching the age of 16 and then starting to consume significantly more alcohol and committing more crimes.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

The [Deutsche Hauptstelle für Suchtfragen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Hauptstelle_für_Suchtfragen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Deutsche Hauptstelle für Suchtfragen (page does not exist)") [[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche%20Hauptstelle%20für%20Suchtfragen "de:Deutsche Hauptstelle für Suchtfragen")] (German Centre for Addiction Issues) recommends raising the drinking age for all alcoholic beverages in Germany to 18 years.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

The [German Cancer Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Cancer_Research_Center "German Cancer Research Center") calls for raising the drinking age in Germany to a uniform 18 years for all types of alcoholic beverages.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In a representative survey conducted on [YouGov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouGov "YouGov") in 2015, a majority of the 1252 participants were in favor of raising the minimum age for light alcoholic beverages in Germany to 18.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

In a survey conducted by the [MDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitteldeutscher_Rundfunk "Mitteldeutscher Rundfunk"), 85% of the approximately 19,000 participants were in favor of a general ban on the sale of alcohol to under-18-year-olds in Germany.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

[Burkhard Blienert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burkhard_Blienert "Burkhard Blienert"), Federal Government Commissioner for Addiction and Drug Issues since 2022, spoke on the subject of the drinking age in Germany and is in favor of raising it to 18 for all types of alcoholic beverages and abolishing the regulation of "begleitetes Trinken" ("accompanied drinking") from 14 years of age.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

### Enforcement

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Enforcement")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Jugendschutz_Alkohol_01.jpg/250px-Jugendschutz_Alkohol_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jugendschutz_Alkohol_01.jpg)

Police operation in Bensheim (Hesse). Several young people have to dispose of illegally obtained alcoholic beverages in the sewers, because they have not reached the required age limit.

In 2008, the federal state of [Lower Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Saxony "Lower Saxony") started a series of [trap purchases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_operation "Sting operation"), conducted by specially trained police cadets, aged 16 or 17, who pose as customers. In 77% of all tests alcohol was sold illegally in shops, filling stations and kiosks. In 2009, about 3000 trap purchases were carried out in Lower Saxony, in 1327 cases (44%) alcohol was sold without age verification to underage persons. Hundreds of summary proceedings led to administrative fines ranging from 500 to 3000 euros. The standard rate for the illegal sale of one bottle of spirits is 1500 euros. Thus, alcohol trap purchases bring a return of around €2 million annually. Other German states, especially [Schleswig-Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schleswig-Holstein "Schleswig-Holstein"), are considering implementing the Lower Saxony model, but states like [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), [Brandenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg "Brandenburg"), [Saxony-Anhalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxony-Anhalt "Saxony-Anhalt"), [Thuringia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuringia "Thuringia") and [Baden-Württemberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baden-Württemberg "Baden-Württemberg") object to it.

Violation of restraints will involve prosecution for vendors who sell alcohol to underage persons and also for bystanders who do not intervene in underage drinking. Although restrictions are nationwide and well-known, some salespersons violate the law at times. Minors themselves can never be prosecuted for alcohol consumption under age. Supermarkets and stores generally check minors for their identity card. The law is less thoroughly enforced in many bars and restaurants, but this can vary by location.

### Fines for violation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Fines for violation")]

Under the *Protection of Young Persons Act* selling, furnishing and supplying alcoholic beverages in licensed premises, at points of sales or elsewhere in public by a person over the age of 18 years to a person under the required age limits is considered a misdemeanor. Violation can result in fines up to €50,000.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

The "Bußgeldkatalog" of each state sets the possible fines for each violation of the act and varies slightly by state. In the state of Baden-Württemberg the Bußgeldkatalog for violation against the "Protection of Young Persons Act" provides following fines:[[26]](#cite_note-Bußgeldkatalog_JuSchG-26)

| Misdemeanor | Law | Possible fine (retailer & business operator) | Standard fine (retailer & business operator) | Possible fine (other) | Standard fine (other) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Selling or serving spirits or food products, containing more than insignificant quantities of spirits, to a child under 14 years of age | § 9 Sec. 1 JuSchG | €1,000 - €4,000 | €3,000 | €300 - €1,000 | €500 |
| Selling or serving spirits or food products, containing more than insignificant quantities of spirits, to a young person over the age of 14 but under the age of 18 years | § 9 Sec. 1 JuSchG | €700 - €3,500 | €2,000 | €100 - €500 | €300 |
| Selling or serving beer, wine, wine-like beverages or sparkling wine or mixtures of beer, wine, wine-like beverages or sparkling wine and soft drinks, to a child under 14 years of age | § 9 Sec. 1 JuSchG | €700 - €3,500 | €2,500 | €100 - €500 | €300 |
| Selling or serving beer, wine, wine-like beverages or sparkling wine or mixtures of beer, wine, wine-like beverages or sparkling wine and soft drinks, to an unaccompanied young person over 14 years but under 16 years of age | § 9 Sec. 1 JuSchG | €500 - €3,000 | €2,000 | €100 - €500 | €300 |

## Other legislation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Other legislation")]

### Alcohol consumption in public

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Alcohol consumption in public")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Alkoholverbot_Nikolaistra%C3%9Fe_G%C3%B6ttingen.jpg/250px-Alkoholverbot_Nikolaistra%C3%9Fe_G%C3%B6ttingen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alkoholverbot_Nikolaistraße_Göttingen.jpg)

Alcohol ban in Göttingen's Nikolaistraße

Public parties are prohibited nationally on [Good Friday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday "Good Friday"), and regionally on other holidays such as [All Saints' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Saints'_Day "All Saints' Day"). Buying alcohol remains possible at these times. The government maintains the right to restrict or ban the sale of alcohol for a certain time to maintain public order (§ 19 GastG).[[27]](#cite_note-27)

Beyond this, Germany has very few restrictions on alcohol consumption in public. Exceptions are sometimes made in the context of [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") matches involving rival teams, where police executives may ban the sale of alcoholic drinks inside stadiums and deny entrance to drunk people. In 2009, the private railway company [Metronom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metronom_Eisenbahngesellschaft "Metronom Eisenbahngesellschaft"), which operates in parts of Northern Germany, introduced a much-discussed complete ban on alcohol onboard their trains.[[28]](#cite_note-28) Some cities have banned alcohol consumption in certain areas and at certain times, such as [Göttingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Göttingen "Göttingen") in Nikolaistraße on Saturdays and Sundays between 00:00 and 08:00, or in [Hannover Hauptbahnhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannover_Hauptbahnhof "Hannover Hauptbahnhof") (outside the existing bars and restaurants) until 2011 when the ban was repealed.

Until 2009, it was acceptable for employees in many fields of work (especially builders, gardeners and manual labourers) to consume medium quantities of alcohol during work hours. However, occupational safety legislation has since tightened down and has induced a significant decrease of alcohol consumption during working hours.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

### Drinking and driving

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Drinking and driving")]

Germany has laws regarding operation of motor vehicles under the influence of alcohol and other psychoactive substances. There are a series of different rules and penalties tied to various blood alcohol levels.

* 0.0‰ for those under the age of 21 or with less than two years' experience, professional drivers, bus drivers, lorry drivers, and drivers transporting passengers commercially;
* 0.3‰ in conjunction with an accident or traffic offense;
* 0.5‰ otherwise.
* 1.6‰ for cyclists, where not in conjunction with any other traffic offense or accident. From 1.6‰, cyclists face the same penalties as driving a car at that limit.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

Penalties start at a €500 fine and one-month licence suspension. Above 0.11%, the penalty is a €500 fine and the withdrawal of the driving licence for at least six months, but usually about one year (penalty is set by the court); from 0.16%, reissue of the licence requires a successful [medical-psychological assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical-psychological_assessment_(Germany) "Medical-psychological assessment (Germany)") (MPU), often referred to as the *Idiotentest* ("idiot test"). For violators above 1.1‰ within ten years of a prior offence above 0.5‰, there is a minimum €1000 fine and a one-year licence withdrawal; the driver has to successfully pass an MPU and is required to prove to the court that they have been sober for the last twelve months, before they can get their licence back. For repeat offenses, the fine is multiplied by the ordinal of the offence (doubled, tripled, etc.), regardless of the amount by which the driver was over the limit. These minimum penalties are usually exceeded by the German courts. From 1.1‰, the courts usually also require the DUI offender to do unpaid community service.

The same rules for operating an automobile while intoxicated also apply to [e-scooters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-scooters "E-scooters").[[31]](#cite_note-31)

In addition to fines, impaired drivers are generally given [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_system_(driving) "Point system (driving)") in the *Fahreignungsregister* ("driving aptitude register", colloquially *Verkehrssünderkartei*, "traffic sinner index"), which is managed by the *Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt* ("[Federal Motor Transport Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Motor_Transport_Authority "Federal Motor Transport Authority")") in [Flensburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flensburg "Flensburg").

It is legal to consume alcohol while driving, provided the driver remains under the legal blood alcohol limits.[[32]](#cite_note-ams-32)

### Licensing laws

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Licensing laws")]

#### Off premises

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Off premises")]

Germany does not require any licenses for the production, wholesale, or retail sale of alcoholic beverages.[[33]](#cite_note-eurocaregermany-33)[[34]](#cite_note-ecreport-34)

#### On premises

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: On premises")]

The permit is not required if alcohol-free beverages, free samples, prepared food is sold or administered or in connection with an accommodation establishment beverages and prepared food is delivered to residents.[[35]](#cite_note-2GastG-35) Every other establishment which does not apply to this scheme requires a *[Gaststättenkonzession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaststättenkonzession?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gaststättenkonzession (page does not exist)") [[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaststättenkonzession "de:Gaststättenkonzession")]*. A [liquor license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquor_license "Liquor license") is generally required when alcoholic beverages are served or sold for consumption on premises.

##### Rules and regulations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Rules and regulations")]

On-licence premises have to place a clearly legible notice with the restrictions of the Protection of Young Persons Act *(Jugendschutzgesetz)*[[36]](#cite_note-3GastG-36) and the bartender must ensure that alcoholic beverages may not be sold or served to underage or visibly intoxicated persons.[[37]](#cite_note-20GastG-37) Operator of a licensed premises are not allowed to force their customers to buy a meal with a drink or change prices if a customer does not order a meal. Changing prices if a customer does not buy an alcoholic drink is also against the law, and every licensee must ensure that there is at least one non alcoholic drink that is cheaper than the cheapest alcoholic drink.[[37]](#cite_note-20GastG-37)

##### Closing hours

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alcohol_laws_in_Germany&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Closing hours")]

[Closing hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_call_(bar_term) "Last call (bar term)") for bars and [discotheques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discotheque "Discotheque") are appointed mostly by state legislation. Within the past ten years, many states have abolished the closing hours for licensed establishments. Most states have retained the so-called *Putzstunde* ("Cleaning hour"), which refers to the 1–2 hours (usually between 5 AM and 6 AM) during which licensed premises are not allowed to serve their customers.

In contrast to many other countries, legislation is relatively lenient and not designed to keep young people away from alcohol, but rather intended to teach them an appropriate approach to alcohol consumption, which is reflected by one of the lowest drinking ages in the world., Due to the low taxation on alcohol, low drinking age and lax regulations regarding availability, as well as a supposed social trivialization of the risks and harmfulness of alcohol in the country, Germany has been referred to as a paradise for drinkers., In Germany, underage drinking in private is not regulated by a specific legal restriction., At 14 – Minors are allowed to consume and possess undistilled alcoholic beverages, such as beer and wine in public places, bars or restaurants, as long as they are in the company and have the permission of a Custodial Person., Germany does not require any licenses for the production, wholesale, or retail sale of alcoholic beverages.
args.summary:
The Wikipedia article on "Alcohol laws in Germany" explains that German alcohol regulation focuses primarily on youth protection and is relatively lenient compared to many other countries, reflecting one of the lowest drinking ages in the world. Tax rates are below European averages, public drinking is generally legal, and the alcohol industry has prevented stricter regulations. Germany has the fifth highest per capita alcohol consumption worldwide, with high rates of teenage drinking.

**Drinking Ages** (regulated by the Protection of Young Persons Act / Jugendschutzgesetz):
- **At 14**: Minors may consume beer and wine in public if accompanied by and with permission of a custodial person ("begleitetes Trinken").
- **At 16**: Minors may consume beer and wine in public without supervision.
- **At 18**: Adults may consume distilled spirits.
- These limits do not apply to married adolescents.

**Debate on Raising the Drinking Age**: Various health organizations (German Centre for Addiction Issues, German Cancer Research Center), the Federal Drug Commissioner, and public surveys support raising the drinking age to 18 for all alcoholic beverages. Some politicians have called for abolishing "accompanied drinking" from age 14.

**Enforcement**: Trap purchases by police cadets in Lower Saxony found 44% of vendors sold alcohol illegally to minors in 2009. Fines for violations can reach up to €50,000, with standard fines ranging from €500 to €3,000 depending on the offense.

**Other Legislation**:
- **Public consumption**: Mostly unrestricted, with some local bans and a national prohibition on public parties on Good Friday.
- **Drinking and driving**: 0.0‰ for novice drivers and professionals; 0.3‰ with an accident or offense; 0.5‰ general limit; 1.6‰ for cyclists. Penalties include fines, license suspension, and mandatory medical-psychological assessment (MPU).
- **Licensing**: No license required for off-premises alcohol sales. On-premises requires a Gaststättenkonzession (liquor license). Closing hours vary by state, with several states having abolished them entirely.

# Alcohol and Young Adults Ages 18 to 25

**Updated:** March 2026

[Spanish / En español](/alcohols-effects-health/alcohol-topics-z/datos-y-estadisticas-sobre-el-alcohol/el-alcohol-y-los-adultos-jovenes-de-18-25-anos)

## Prevalence of Past-Month Drinking

According to the 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), 16.6 million young adults ages 18 to 25 (47.5% in this age group) reported that they drank alcohol in the past month.1,2 This includes:

* 8.2 million males ages 18 to 25 (46.7% in this age group)1,2
* 8.4 million females ages 18 to 25 (48.3% in this age group)1,2

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 4.2 million full-time college students ages 18 to 25 (46.6%) and 11.8 million other persons of the same age (47.7%) reported that they drank alcohol in the past month.3

## Prevalence of Past-Month Binge Drinking

Image

![Alcohol and young adults past month binge drinking; 26.5% males vs. 26.9% females](/sites/default/files/styles/image_425/public/2024%20NSDUH%20Young%20Adults%20Binge_0.png?itok=sGGjlVI1)

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 9.3 million young adults ages 18 to 25 (26.7% in this age group) reported binge drinking in the past month ([see glossary](/alcohols-effects-health/alcohol-topics-z/alcohol-facts-and-statistics/glossary "Glossary") for definition of binge drinking).4,5 This includes:

* 4.7 million males ages 18 to 25 (26.5% in this age group)4,5
* 4.7 million females ages 18 to 25 (26.9% in this age group)4,5

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 2.3 million full-time college students ages 18 to 25 (25.0%) and 6.7 million other persons of the same age (27.3%) reported binge drinking in the past month.3

## Prevalence of Past-Month Heavy Alcohol Use

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 2.1 million young adults ages 18 to 25 (6.0% in this age group) reported heavy alcohol use in the past month ([see glossary](/alcohols-effects-health/alcohol-topics-z/alcohol-facts-and-statistics/glossary "Glossary") for definition of heavy alcohol use).6,7 This includes:

* 1.2 million males ages 18 to 25 (6.6% in this age group)6,7
* 940,000 females ages 18 to 25 5.4% in this age group)6,7

According to the 2024 NSDUH, 456,000 full-time college students ages 18 to 25 (5.0%) and 1.6 million other persons of the same age (6.5%) reported heavy drinking in the past month.3

## Prevalence of High-Intensity Drinking

According to the 2024 Monitoring the Future (MTF) Panel Study, 4.7% of full-time college students and 7.2% of non-college young adults one to four years beyond high school engaged in high-intensity drinking (10+ drinks in a row) in the last two weeks.8

## Consequences of Alcohol Use

* Alcohol is a factor in the deaths of thousands of young people every year in the United States. The most recent National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism statistics estimate that this includes 1,519 college students ages 18 to 24 and 2,586 persons the same age who die from alcohol-related unintentional injuries, including motor vehicle crashes.9
* According to the 2024 NSDUH, 14.4% of adults ages 18 to 25 met the criteria for past-year alcohol use disorder (AUD).10 Within this age group, 14.5% of full-time college students ages 18 to 25 and 15.3% of other persons of the same age met the criteria for AUD.11
* Although estimating the number of alcohol-related sexual assaults is exceptionally challenging because sexual assault is typically underreported, researchers have confirmed a long-standing finding that one in five college women experience sexual assault during their time in college.12A majority of sexual assaults in college involve alcohol or other substances.13,14 Research continues to better understand the relationship between alcohol and sexual assault among college students. Additional national survey data are needed to better estimate the number of alcohol-related assaults.
* An analysis of about 2000 college students from 46 schools found that 4.3% of sophomores and juniors reported being physically harmed, 14.3% experienced verbal abuse, 13.0% experienced emotional abuse related to someone else's drinking.15

According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), many (but not all) NSDUH estimates from 2024 are comparable with 2022, 2023, and updated 2021 estimates. However, 2021–2024 estimates are not comparable with 2020 or prior years’ estimates. Please see the [2024 NSDUH Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/data-we-collect/nsduh-national-survey-drug-use-and-health/national-releases/2024) and section 2.3.4 of the [2024 Methodological Summary and Definitions](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/data-we-collect/nsduh-national-survey-drug-use-and-health/methodology/2024) report for more details.

## REVIEW article

# Too young to pour: the global crisis of underage alcohol use

Susanna Esposito 1\*

Beatrice Rita Campana 1

Alberto Argentiero 1

Marco Masetti 1

Valentina Fainardi 1

Nicola Principi 2

1. Pediatric Clinic, Department of Medicine and Surgery, University of Parma, Parma, Italy

2. Università degli Studi di Milano, Milan, Italy

Article metrics

## Abstract

**Background:**

Underage alcohol consumption remains a critical global public health concern, contributing to a wide spectrum of short- and long-term health risks. Despite age-based legal restrictions, alcohol persists as the most commonly used psychoactive substance among minors, outpacing tobacco, cannabis, and other drugs. Early initiation of alcohol use is strongly associated with heightened risks of addiction, impaired brain development, mental health disorders, and engagement in high-risk behaviors such as unintentional injuries, violence, and academic underperformance. Most research has focused on adolescents, while data on younger children remain scarce. Moreover, methodological inconsistencies in defining and measuring alcohol use across countries complicate international comparisons and the evaluation of policy interventions.

**Methods:**

This narrative review synthesizes contemporary literature on the epidemiology, determinants, and consequences of underage alcohol use. It examines genetic predispositions, family dynamics, peer influence, socioeconomic context, mental health, and exposure to alcohol-related media and advertising. It also evaluates the effectiveness of intervention strategies, including parental engagement, school-based education, extracurricular activities, community-level regulation, and professional health services.

**Results:**

Evidence highlights significant variability in the prevalence of underage drinking across regions, influenced by cultural, legal, and socioeconomic factors. Parental modeling, permissive attitudes, and weakened family structures are major contributors, while peer pressure and media exposure further normalize early alcohol use. Although various prevention strategies have demonstrated short-term benefits (particularly those involving active parental involvement and skill-based school programs), long-term effectiveness is limited due to inconsistent implementation, lack of standardization, and inadequate policy enforcement. Community-level interventions, such as increasing the legal drinking age and conducting compliance checks, have shown measurable success, but are underutilized in many regions.

**Conclusion:**

Addressing underage drinking requires a coordinated, multifactorial strategy. Broader investment in early prevention, standardized assessment tools, and targeted research on younger populations is essential. Strengthening policy enforcement and cross-sector collaboration will be critical to mitigate this growing public health challenge.

## 1 Background

Although with differences among countries, alcohol consumption is a significant clinical and public health concern worldwide. It is associated with severe health risks, including liver damage, cancer development, cardiovascular complications, and neurological and mental health disorders. Additionally, alcohol use can lead to profound social, occupational, and relationship problems, often resulting in premature death ([1](#ref1)). The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that in 2019, alcohol-related deaths reached 2.6 million globally. Furthermore, approximately 400 million people lived with alcohol use disorders, with 209 million diagnosed as alcohol dependent ([2](#ref2)).

Among alcohol drinkers, a substantial portion consists of school children and adolescents. Alcohol is the most widely used substance among these age groups, surpassing tobacco, nicotine vaping, and marijuana ([3](#ref3)). While overall alcohol use is typically more prevalent among adults, studies indicate that adolescents and young adults may engage in riskier patterns of use, such as binge drinking, at comparable or higher rates than adults ([4–7](#ref4)). According to the most recent WHO/Europe report, over half of surveyed 15-year-olds had already experimented with alcohol ([8](#ref8)). In the United States, the 2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health found that 12.6 million individuals aged 12 to 20 (33.1% of this age group) had consumed alcohol at least once in their lives ([9](#ref9)). Additionally, approximately 4,000 people under the age of 21 died from excessive alcohol use ([3](#ref3)).

These statistics are particularly alarming, given that most countries prohibit the sale, provision, or offering of alcoholic products to minors, with variations in the legal drinking age ([10](#ref10)). Despite these legal restrictions, underage alcohol use remains widespread and poses severe health consequences distinct from those observed in adults. Children who engage in heavy drinking are at a significantly higher risk of developing alcohol dependency and substance abuse disorders later in life. Moreover, alcohol-related chronic conditions such as liver cirrhosis, cardiovascular diseases, and certain cancers manifest earlier in children than in adults ([11](#ref11), [12](#ref12)).

Additionally, mental health problems are significantly more common and severe among adolescents who consume alcohol. Adolescence is a crucial period for biopsychosocial development, and alcohol use during this stage can disrupt brain maturation, leading to cognitive impairments and learning difficulties. Furthermore, early alcohol consumption is linked to higher engagement in risky behaviors, including motor vehicle accidents, homicides, falls, burns, drownings, and suicides. Underage alcohol abuse also imposes a substantial burden on public resources by increasing healthcare expenditures, contributing to educational failures, and escalating the demand for mental health services ([13](#ref13)).

Despite these concerns, the epidemiology of alcohol use in children, particularly the youngest, remains poorly understood. Additionally, the social and economic factors contributing to underage drinking among very young individuals are not well-documented. This precludes identification of the best measures capable of preventing and reduce underage alcohol drinking. Finally, targeted initiatives by health authorities to combat alcohol consumption by children and adolescents are relatively uncommon worldwide. A WHO report indicated that in 2017, approximately 50% of countries, including several high-income nations, lacked programs for the treatment of children with alcohol and substance use disorders ([14](#ref14)). This paper aims to summarize the current knowledge on underage alcohol drinking in children and adolescents in order to favor the identification of the problems whose solution can reduce epidemiology and consequences of this significant pediatric problems.

## 2 Methods

This is a narrative review that intends to synthesize the existing knowledge on underage alcohol consumption, including epidemiological data, determinants of use, and available interventions. No primary data were collected; rather, the study relied on a comprehensive literature search of empirical research, governmental reports, and authoritative health organization publications. A literature search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using predefined keywords such as “underage drinking,” “adolescent alcohol use,” “youth alcohol consumption,” “alcohol-related harm in minors,” and “prevention programs for underage drinking.” The search covered publications from January 2000 to January 2025, with additional seminal and policy-relevant studies included irrespective of publication date. Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers to assess eligibility. Full-text articles were retrieved for studies that met the inclusion criteria or where eligibility was uncertain. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus.

Inclusion criteria prioritized peer-reviewed empirical studies, government reports, and publications by international health organizations (e.g., WHO, CDC) that reported on prevalence, determinants, or interventions related to underage alcohol use. Studies were appraised based on methodological rigor (e.g., study design, sample size, measurement validity), relevance to the research question, and geographical diversity. Particular emphasis was placed on studies offering cross-national comparisons or policy evaluations.

Statistical data were extracted from authoritative sources to ensure accuracy in prevalence estimates and health outcomes. Program and policy evaluations were assessed based on implementation fidelity, reported effectiveness, and long-term impact. Although this review is not a meta-analysis, it follows structured narrative synthesis principles to ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Epidemiology of alcohol use in younger children and adolescents

Numerous studies have documented that many children consume alcohol; however, the precise epidemiology of underage alcohol consumption across different social and economic contexts remains poorly defined. Significant variations exist among countries, even among those with similar general characteristics. In the United States, results from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health have indicated that in 2021, among people aged 12 to 20, 15.1% (5.9 million) were past month alcohol users. Estimates of binge alcohol use and heavy alcohol use in the past month in the same population were 8.3% (3.2 million) and 1.6% (613,000), respectively ([15](#ref15)). Significant differences among states were reported. Vermont had the highest rate of underage alcohol users, with nearly 25% consuming alcohol and 14% binge-drinking in the month before the survey. Mississippi, the state with the lowest underage consumption, at 9.7% for use and 5.4% for binge drinking ([16](#ref16)).

In the European Union (EU), a 2019 survey revealed that 37.4% of children aged 15–16 years reported engaging in at least one episode of heavy drinking, defined as consuming five or more drinks on one occasion within the past 30 days. Notably, prevalence rates varied among Nordic countries, with lower rates observed in Iceland (8%), Norway (16%), Sweden (20%), and Finland (22%), but very high rates in Denmark, where the percentage of heavy drinkers was the highest (59%) among all European nations. Rates above the European average were also observed in Germany, Austria, Slovakia, and Croatia, where over 45% of adolescents engaged in heavy drinking ([17](#ref17)).

Strong differences among countries were also reported in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 141 studies conducted in sub-Saharan Africa between 2018 and 2024, revealing varying lifetime and 6-month prevalence rates of alcohol use among children aged 10–17 years. Lifetime prevalence ranged from 13.2% in Ghana to 71.0% in Benin, while 6-month prevalence ranged from 1.2% in Uganda to 80.6% in Zambia and 46.3% in Seychelles ([18](#ref18)).

Studies conducted in Southern American nations confirm that although a notable number of children and adolescents consume alcohol in all the countries, significant variation in prevalence among different countries can be demonstrated. A survey carried out in 14 Latin American countries ([19](#ref19)) revealed that the lifetime prevalence of alcohol use among adolescents aged 14–17 years was 39% in Bolivia and 78.2% in Uruguay. Uruguay and Bolivia also reported the highest and lowest prevalence of alcohol use in the last year (67 and 28%) and the last month (50 and 16%), respectively. In Argentina, the lifetime, last year, and last month prevalence of alcohol use (63, 53, and 42%, respectively) was comparable to Paraguay (60, 49, and 40%), Chile (68, 57, and 40%), and Brazil (69, 67, and 48%). Other studies in Brazil ([20](#ref20)) and Mexico ([21](#ref21)) reported similar prevalence rates. Several factors contribute to these differences, including national regulations regarding alcohol consumption, heterogeneous study populations, and variability of methods for measuring alcohol consumption and duration. These inconsistencies complicate comparisons across studies and may impede adolescent research and policy planning.

Strict alcohol regulations can effectively deter underage drinking. Research indicates that measures, such as setting a minimum purchase age, reducing the density of alcohol outlets, and limiting sale days and hours can significantly decrease alcohol consumption among minors. Conversely, when state monopolies are replaced with private liquor stores or a licensed system, significant issues may arise. A study conducted in Sweden revealed that the privatization of the Swedish alcohol retail market was associated with a higher density of outlets, longer hours or more days of sale, changes in price, and an increase in consumption ([22](#ref22)). However, legal drinking age policies differ significantly among countries. Some nations, primarily those with majority Muslim populations, impose stricter prohibitions on alcohol for the entire population. Conversely, in most industrialized countries, the minimum legal drinking age is 18 years, while in the United States, it is 21. Exceptions that facilitate alcohol use are common; for example, in the United Kingdom, where the legal drinking age is 18 years, alcohol consumption is permitted for 16-17-year-olds during meals when accompanied by an adult ([23](#ref23)).

Regarding the heterogeneity of study populations, it is important to note that most studies focus on adolescents. However, the definition of adolescence varies. Generally, studies include individuals aged 10–18 years, but some extend the age range to 9–24 years, thereby increasing the number of participants classified as adolescents ([24](#ref24)). Additionally, studies evaluating the initiation of alcohol use sometimes include much younger children. For example, research conducted in Uganda ([25](#ref25)) and Peru ([26](#ref26)) included children as young as 5 years old. Since the risk of alcohol use among these younger children is low, the global prevalence of alcohol consumption in pediatrics is lower than that reported in studies that enroll only adolescents.

The definition of alcohol consumption also influences epidemiological study results. Various criteria are used, including frequency of alcohol use, drinking quantity, weekly drinking, binge drinking, drunkenness, and alcohol-related problems. A greater prevalence of alcohol use is observed when it is defined as the intake of any alcohol, even in minimal amounts, while stricter definitions that account for blood alcohol concentration yield lower prevalence rates ([27](#ref27)).

Alcohol consumption patterns among children can differ by sex, race, ethnicity, and study population composition. A study conducted across 44 countries in Europe, Central Asia, and Canada during the 2021/2022 period found that, in some countries, alcohol consumption was slightly more prevalent among girls than boys ([28](#ref28)). In the United States, multiple studies have reported that White youth generally exhibit higher lifetime and 30-day drinking prevalence compared to African American youth. However, their alcohol use rates are similar to or lower than those of Hispanic youth, who often report higher levels of alcohol consumption ([29](#ref29)).
